P2500.d: P2500 points to the L line, the turn-on wire between engine module and alternator regulator that on many older layouts also runs through the charge warning lamp. The module reads back the voltage on this wire; when it stays below the expected level, for instance because the line is chafed to ground or the regulator holds it down, this code is logged.
s: Battery or charge warning lamp on
Battery voltage falls while driving
Hard or no start after some time
c: L wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Alternator regulator faulty and pulling the L terminal low
Corroded or loose plug at the alternator
Output stage for the L line in the engine module defective

P2501.d: With P2501 the engine module sees too much voltage on the L line to the alternator regulator. The wire is then either touching a battery-fed conductor, or the module cannot pull it down because the regulator side or the lamp path is open, so the line floats up to supply level.
s: Charge lamp does not light during the bulb check or stays on
Charging voltage unusually high or not controlled
Battery drains if charging stops
c: L wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Break in the L circuit or plug off at the alternator

P2502.d: P2502 is the general charging-system code: the engine module compares the voltage the generator actually delivers with what it has requested and finds a mismatch that it does not classify as simply too low or too high. Mazda uses it as a malfunction in the voltage produced by the generator.
s: Charge warning lamp on while driving
Fluctuating battery voltage, flickering lights
Battery not fully charged
c: Alternator or regulator not reaching the requested voltage
High resistance at ground or B+ connections (Mazda mild hybrid DC-DC converter)
Slipping drive belt or worn tensioner
Battery with internal fault distorting the charging voltage

P2503.d: P2503 means the charging output is below target: with the engine running the module expects the generator to lift system voltage, but it stays too low. FCA calls the code Charging System Output Low.
s: Battery lamp and check engine lamp on
Dim lights, electrical consumers dropping out
Engine stalls or will not start
c: Loose or burnt B+ connection between alternator and fuse box
Failed overrunning pulley or slipping belt

P2504.d: P2504 is logged when the charging output overshoots: the measured voltage rises above what the module asked the generator to produce. FCA names it Charging System Output High and publishes several cases.
s: Check engine lamp, sometimes battery lamp
Very bright lights, bulbs failing early
No crank in connection-related cases
c: High resistance at B+ fuse array or ground straps distorting the reading
Battery current or voltage sensor delivering wrong values

P2505.d: P2505 covers the supply inputs of the engine module in general. GM documents it in the 2014 diesel engine table 14OBDG04: the module checks its permanent battery feed, the line that keeps the engine-off timer alive while the ignition is off.
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Often no drivability complaint
Learned values may be lost
c: Battery disconnected or permanent-feed fuse removed or blown
Open or corroded permanent supply wire or connector
Supply monitoring inside the module defective

P2506.d: P2506 is the plausibility variant: the supply reaching the engine module is electrically present but its value or behaviour does not fit the operating state. No passenger-car maker publishes how it detects this.
s: Check engine lamp (Ford lists it as MIL code)
Sporadic stalling or restarts of the module possible
c: Resistance in supply fuse, relay contact or connector
Excessive current drawn through the module supply (Deutz)
Internal supply monitoring of the module faulty

P2507.d: P2507 reports that a supply input of the engine module sits too low. Makers read this differently.
s: Often no symptom, code found during service (Mazda)
Several warning lamps, blank displays
No-start in severe cases
c: Supply fuse missing, pulled for transport or not fully seated
Weak battery or voltage dips during repeated starts
Corroded supply wire, ground or relay contact
Internal 5 V supply of the module failing (Ford diesel)

P2508.d: P2508 is set when a supply input of the engine module reads above its permitted range. Ford documents it for the 2023 6.7 L Power Stroke diesel: the module checks its internal 5 V supply rail and flags P2508 once that rail exceeds 5.5 V, with continuous monitoring, roughly 5 s to mature, and the module awake (key on, running or after-run).
s: Check engine lamp
Other diagnostics such as the DEF quality test suspended
Erratic sensor values possible
c: Internal 5 V regulator of the engine module defective
Supply or sensor wire shorted to battery voltage
Overvoltage from charging fault or jump start

P2509.d: P2509 records a brief loss of the engine module's supply, a dropout rather than a lasting low or high value. Two Cummins-powered pickups show how easily it appears.
s: MIL on, often without drivability complaint
Code appears right after battery work
c: Battery disconnected before the module finished its after-run
Loose battery clamp, ground or supply connector
Module software too sensitive, fixed by reflash (Ram 6.7 L)

P250A.d: P250A is the general circuit code for the engine oil level sensor, a unit in the sump that today mostly measures by heated element or ultrasound and often reports oil temperature as well. Its use varies.
s: Oil level warning or message in the cluster
Oil level display missing or wrong
With harness damage, further engine codes and stalling (GM)
c: Sensor harness chafed or pinched (GM X154 jumper harness)
Engine oil overfilled, sensor reading out of range (Mazda CX-9)
Oil level sensor defective or leaking at its seal
Corroded or oily connector at the sump

P250B.d: P250B fires when the oil level sensor answers electrically but its reading is implausible, for instance a level that jumps, stays frozen while the engine runs, or contradicts the value after a stop. Continuous sensors see a lower level in operation than at rest, so the plausibility logic has to account for running state, temperature and inclination.
s: Oil level message without real oil loss
Level display jumps or stays fixed
c: Plausibility logic in the engine module too strict, fixed by update (Alfa Romeo)
Sensor element aged or contaminated by sludge
Oil level far outside the calibrated range after a service

P250C.d: P250C means the oil level sensor's signal line is pulled too low, the classic picture of a short to ground or, depending on the input design, a break that lets the line drop. Deutz describes its P250C-00 the same way: level sensor line grounded or interrupted.
s: Oil level warning lamp on
No oil level reading in the cluster
c: Signal wire shorted to ground near the sump
Open circuit or unplugged sensor connector
Warning logic in the engine module, fixed by reflash (Hyundai 2.0 Nu)

P250D.d: P250D is stored when the oil level sensor line rises above its valid range. The usual explanation is contact with a positive conductor; with pull-up inputs an interrupted line or missing sensor ground can also drive the signal high.
s: Oil level warning or message
Level display permanently at maximum
c: Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Sensor ground open or signal line interrupted

P250E.d: P250E flags an oil level signal that drops out or jumps in an unrealistic way while the circuit otherwise looks intact. Typical sources are a loose terminal, a wire that breaks only under engine movement, or a sensor that loses its echo or heating cycle intermittently.
s: Oil level message appears and disappears
Jumping level display
c: Loose or oily terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from engine movement
Sensor losing its measuring cycle sporadically

P250F.d: P250F is not a wiring code: the oil level sensor works, and the measured level is below the minimum. Mazda used it on 2021 models with the 2.5 L turbo (Mazda3, Mazda6, CX-30, CX-5, CX-9) where a low-oil message and the check engine light appeared after roughly 5,000 to 7,500 km without visible leaks; Mazda suspected oil entering the combustion chambers past damaged valve stem seals and first topped up free of charge.
s: Low engine oil message and check engine light
Oil level near or below minimum on the dipstick
c: Oil burned past valve stem seals or piston rings
External oil leak or too little oil after a service
Warning logic triggering with correct level, fixed by update (Hyundai)

P2510.d: P2510 judges whether the main relay of the engine module behaves as commanded, based on what the module senses on the switched supply. GM's 2014 diesel tables describe two checks.
s: MIL after two trips (GM type B)
Battery drain if the relay stays closed
Lost adaptations if the relay opens too early
c: Main relay contacts welded or sticking
Relay dropping out early (weak coil, poor socket contact)
Battery disconnected or supply lost during after-run
Relay driver or EEPROM handling in the module faulty

P2511.d: P2511 covers short dropouts on the line through which the engine module reads back the output of its main relay. The relay is commanded on, yet the sensed voltage briefly vanishes and returns, typical of a chattering contact, a cracked solder joint in the relay or a loose terminal in the fuse box.
s: Engine may stall briefly or hesitate
Several modules logging voltage-related codes
c: Worn or chattering main relay contact
Loose relay socket or fuse box terminal

P2512.d: P2512 concerns the wired request line between the event data recorder and the engine module. The recorder, normally part of the airbag control unit, stores a short history of speed, throttle, brake and other pre-crash data when it senses a crash or near-crash, and needs powertrain values for that.
s: Code stored without noticeable symptoms
Possibly a service or wrench indicator
c: Request wire broken or connector unplugged
Airbag/recorder module missing, replaced or not configured
Engine module configured for a recorder line that is not fitted

P2513.d: P2513 is set when the event data recorder request line reads too low at the engine module. A wire rubbed through to body ground, a crushed harness after body work, or water in a floor connector are the obvious suspects; a low line may also be read as a permanent request.
s: Code stored without drivability effect
Possibly a service or wrench indicator
c: Moisture or corrosion in an under-floor connector
Recorder or engine module input stage faulty

P2514.d: P2514 tells you the request line between the event data recorder and the engine module sits at too high a level. The recorder, normally housed in the airbag control unit, keeps a short log of speed, pedal and brake data around a collision and fetches engine values through this line.
s: Code stored with no effect on driving
Possibly a wrench or service indicator instead of the check engine light
c: Request wire chafed against a powered circuit
Missing ground or unplugged connector at the airbag/recorder module
Input stage in engine or recorder module faulty

P2515.d: P2515 is the general circuit fault of a second refrigerant pressure sensor, called B. Heat pump systems and vehicles with electric compressors often measure pressure at several points in the circuit; which position is B is up to the maker.
s: A/C does not cool or cools only intermittently
Compressor stays off
Further A/C pressure codes such as P0530 stored
c: Pressure sensor electronics failed (Audi early build sensors)
Connector corroded or wiring to the sensor damaged
Evaluating module (thermal management or engine) faulty

P2516.d: P2516 flags a pressure sensor B whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave like real refrigerant pressure. In GM's hybrid OBD tables sensor B is the low-side sensor, evaluated by the hybrid processor that also runs the electric compressor.
s: A/C cools poorly
Check engine light after two drives (GM type B)
Refrigerant charge diagnosis not completed
c: Pressure sensor stuck at one value
Compressor runs but hardly changes pressure (very low charge, blockage)
High resistance in signal or ground wire

P2517.d: P2517 means the signal of refrigerant pressure sensor B has dropped below its usable floor. GM's hybrid tables, where B is the low-side sensor, compute the ratio of signal to the 5 V reference and fail it below 2 % (0.10 V): in 2019 if that holds for 1.6 s of a 2 s window, in 2016 for 16 of 20 samples, in 2011 for 40 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms; each time type B, so the lamp comes on after two drives.
s: A/C compressor does not switch on
Check engine light after two drives on GM hybrids
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference missing (wire or shared supply pulled down)

P2518.d: P2518 is stored when pressure sensor B reports a signal close to its supply voltage. GM, which uses B for the low-side sensor in its hybrid tables, sets the limit at 98 % of the reference, about 4.90 V.
s: Check engine light after one drive on newer GM hybrids
A/C compressor disabled, no cooling
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector

P2519.d: P2519 covers the general circuit fault of a wired input through which the climate control asks the engine module for compressor operation. The engine module needs this request early, to raise idle speed, add torque reserve and then energise the compressor clutch relay.
s: A/C compressor never engages
Idle speed does not rise when A/C is selected
c: Request wire broken or connector loose
Climate control unit or A/C switch not sending a valid signal

P251A.d: P251A concerns the switch the operator uses to arm the power take-off on a work truck. The control module reads this switch line and only allows PTO mode, often with a raised working idle, when the signal is plausible.
s: PTO cannot be engaged or drops out intermittently
Working idle speed is not raised when PTO is selected
Stored code with normal driving behaviour
c: Poor PTO or engine-to-frame ground (paint under the eyelet, corrosion, bolt bottoming out)
Broken or unplugged wire between PTO enable switch and module
Worn PTO enable switch that no longer makes contact
Faulty connection made during body or equipment installation

P251B.d: With P251B the module reads the PTO enable switch input as stuck at a low level, below what either switch position should produce. A wire chafed through to chassis ground, water in a connector or a switch shorted internally are the usual explanations.
s: PTO will not engage, or engages without being selected
PTO indicator lamp behaves incorrectly
Readiness monitors may stay incomplete
c: Switch signal wire chafed against frame or body
Moisture or corrosion in the switch connector

P251C.d: P251C is logged when the PTO enable switch line sits above its valid window, close to supply voltage. That points to a signal wire touching a battery or ignition feed, a reference that has lost its ground, or a pull-up that the switch can no longer pull down.
s: PTO engages or high idle starts without operator request
PTO cannot be switched off normally
Emissions readiness stays not ready
c: Switch signal wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Missing ground on the switch or module reference
Switch stuck in the applied position

P251D.d: P251D covers the engine shutdown line of a power take-off installation. On trucks with body equipment such as cranes, pumps or aerial devices, a hard-wired signal lets the PTO controller or an equipment stop button tell the engine module to switch the engine off.
s: PTO locked out or equipment will not run
Equipment stop button no longer shuts down the engine
c: Open shutdown wire or loose connector at the body interface
Fault in the body equipment's stop switch or controller output
Shutdown input enabled in calibration but not wired by the upfitter

P251E.d: P251E reports that the PTO engine shutdown input reads too low. Whether low means stop now or all clear depends on the maker's wiring, so the practical effect varies: the module may treat the line as an active stop request and refuse to keep the engine running in PTO mode, or it may simply flag the line as shorted and ignore it.
s: Engine stops or will not stay running while PTO is used
PTO function disabled
c: Shutdown wire chafed through to chassis ground
Corroded connector at the body builder interface
Equipment stop switch shorted to ground

P251F.d: P251F is the high-side fault of the PTO engine shutdown input: the voltage stays near supply level where the module expects a defined switching state. A shutdown wire touching a powered circuit in the body harness, a missing ground on the equipment controller, or an add-on module that drives the line permanently are typical.
s: Engine does not stop when equipment shutdown is triggered
PTO operation blocked
c: Shutdown wire shorted to a powered circuit in the body harness
Retrofitted control module holding the line high

P2520.d: P2520 is set when the voltage on A/C request input A stays below the band the engine module accepts. Depending on whether the input is active-high or active-low, a grounded wire then reads as a permanent request or as none at all – either way the module distrusts it.
s: A/C does not switch on, or compressor runs although A/C is off
Idle speed behaves oddly when the A/C is toggled

P2521.d: With P2521 the engine module sees A/C request input A held above its valid range, typically because the wire touches a supply line, the input has lost its pull-down or the sending control unit drives it permanently high. Two makers list the code by number.
s: A/C compressor runs although A/C is switched off
A/C button has no effect
Raised idle speed without A/C request
c: Request wire shorted to a supply voltage
Climate control unit drives the line permanently high
Code newly reported after an engine software update (Sprinter T21)

P2522.d: P2522 is the general circuit code for a second wired A/C request input, B. Why an engine module would need two such lines is left to each maker; plausible uses are a separate rear evaporator, a second request stage or a redundant line to cross-check input A.
s: A/C function served by input B unavailable
Idle dips when the compressor engages without notice
c: Input B wire broken or connector loose
Sending climate module or switch faulty

P2523.d: P2523 reports that A/C request input B is pulled below its valid range. On the wire level this usually means a conductor grounded against body metal, a sending module whose output transistor has failed shorted, or a wet connector draining the signal.
s: Compressor not engaging or engaging unasked
A/C-related idle compensation missing
c: Input B wire shorted to ground
Output stage of the sending module shorted
Moisture in a connector of the request line

P2524.d: P2524 indicates that A/C request input B reads above the level the engine module treats as valid. A line chafed against battery or ignition feed, an open pull-down inside the module or a control unit that latches its output high are the usual explanations.
s: Compressor engages although not requested
A/C cannot be switched off or on as expected
c: Input B wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage

P2525.d: P2525 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor on a vacuum reservoir. Diesels, and many hybrids and electric drives, lack usable intake vacuum and run a separate pump, often driven from the camshaft or by an electric motor, that fills a reservoir.
s: Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced boost or EGR function in default mode
c: Sensor wiring open or connector loose
Shared 5 V reference disturbed by another sensor

P2526.d: P2526 marks a vacuum reservoir pressure reading that stays inside the electrical range but does not fit the situation, for instance no rise in vacuum after the pump has run, or a value frozen while actuators draw on the reservoir. Because the sensor watches a real system, genuine vacuum faults such as a leaking hose, a worn pump or a cracked reservoir can set it as well as a drifting sensor.
s: Check engine light, often with boost or EGR codes
Weak exhaust brake or reduced power
Hissing noise from a leaking line
c: Leaking vacuum hose, check valve or reservoir
Mechanical or electric vacuum pump delivering too little

P2527.d: P2527 means the signal from the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Whether low volts stand for deep vacuum or for atmospheric pressure depends on the sensor curve, but a reading at the floor is treated as an electrical fault, not as a vacuum value.
s: Check engine light
Boost or EGR control in default mode, less power
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down

P2528.d: P2528 is logged when the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor delivers a voltage near or at its supply, beyond anything the sensing element can output. A signal wire touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken sensor ground, or corrosion bridging pins in the connector are the classic findings.
s: Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced power with actuators in default position
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector

P2529.d: P2529 covers a vacuum reservoir pressure signal that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying wrong. The engine module notices changes faster than a reservoir could physically empty or fill, or brief excursions to the electrical limits that recover again.
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Occasional brief loss of power or boost
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing or wire breaking under engine movement

P252A.d: P252A is the general circuit code for an engine oil quality sensor, a unit in the sump that judges the state of the oil from its physical properties. Hella's PULS+C variant, for example, adds measurements of viscosity, density and permittivity to ultrasonic level sensing, so oil changes can follow real wear instead of a fixed mileage.
s: Oil condition or service interval display missing or showing a fault
Warning message in the instrument cluster, usually without engine light
c: Sensor connector loose, unplugged or corroded by oil and moisture
Broken signal, supply or ground wire near the oil pan
Internal electronics of the oil quality sensor failed

P252B.d: P252B covers an oil quality sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense in context. Plausibility logic can weigh the reported oil properties against oil temperature, time since the last service or the engine's own oil ageing model; a value that stays frozen while conditions change, or leaps after a top-up without reason, is suspect.
s: Oil condition display shows implausible values or a fault message
Service interval calculated inconsistently after an oil change
c: Deposits or sludge on the sensing element distort the measurement
Oil grade or viscosity outside what the sensor calibration expects
Sensor aged or drifting, reading frozen or offset
Plausibility logic in the engine software too strict

P252C.d: P252C is stored when the oil quality sensor's signal sits below the range the engine computer accepts. Typical reasons are a signal wire chafed through to ground, a supply line that has lost its voltage or an internal short in the sensor; depending on the input circuit an open wire can also drag the reading down.
s: Oil condition value missing in the cluster or service menu
Service reminder falls back to fixed intervals or shows a fault
c: Signal wire chafed against the oil pan or engine block (short to ground)
Sensor supply voltage missing (fuse, supply wire)
Internal short in the oil quality sensor

P252D.d: P252D means the oil quality sensor reports a voltage above its valid window. A short of the signal line to a positive conductor, a broken sensor ground or, with pull-up inputs, an interrupted signal wire can all push the value to the upper stop.
s: Warning or blank oil condition value in the cluster
Oil change reminder appears too early, too late or not at all
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply or battery-voltage wire
Sensor ground or signal wire interrupted, connector pin pushed back
Sensor electronics stuck at a high output

P252E.d: P252E points to an oil quality signal that briefly drops out or jumps while the circuit is otherwise intact. Typical sources are a terminal that loses contact when the engine shakes, a harness rubbing on the sump or a sensor whose internal measuring cycle is occasionally disturbed.
s: Oil condition message appears and disappears
Fluctuating oil condition or service interval values
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness rubbing on the oil pan with intermittent contact
Sensor electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration

P252F.d: P252F is not a wiring fault: the level sensor works and reports more oil in the sump than the permitted maximum. Deutz's EMR controller files the condition as P252F-00 under oil level parameter SPN 98 with FMI 15, and Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S code table lists P252F without a lamp entry.
s: Oil level warning in the instrument cluster
Dipstick reading above the maximum mark, oil may smell of fuel
Possible rich mixture codes after long drives
c: Too much oil added at the last oil change or top-up
Fuel dilution from frequent short trips or diesel particulate filter regeneration
Coolant entering the oil (head gasket, oil cooler)

P2530.d: P2530 is the general fault of the hard-wired run signal that tells a powertrain module the ignition switch is in its run position. Modules use this line to wake up, power their outputs and decide when to start their internal shutdown routine; many also cross-check it against the ignition status sent over the network.
s: Warning lamps or stored codes in several modules
Engine may stall or not start
Modules staying awake after key-off
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the run feed
Loose terminal at the module or ignition switch

P2531.d: The engine module logs P2531 if the run-position input stays low although the vehicle state says the ignition is on, for example while the engine runs or the network reports run. The supply side is the usual suspect: an open fuse, a relay that does not pull in, a wire grounded on the body or a switch contact that no longer carries current.
s: MIL on
Engine stalls or will not restart
Several warning lamps or communication codes at once
c: Open fuse in the run circuit
Run signal wire shorted to ground

P2532.d: P2532 means voltage is present on the run-position input when it should be absent, typically after key-off or while the network reports the ignition as off. A run feed backfed through another component, a relay with welded contacts or a wire touching a permanent battery feed can cause it.
s: Battery drained after the vehicle is parked
Modules or fans keep running after key-off
c: Voltage backfeed into the run circuit through another component
Run wire touching a permanent battery feed

P2533.d: P2533 is the general fault of the circuit that is live in both the on and the start position of the ignition switch, often called run/crank. Unlike the pure run line it must stay powered while the starter turns, so modules rely on it to remain awake during cranking.
s: MIL on
Possible no-start or stall during cranking
c: Powertrain module software or parameters (Ford Mach-E 2021, reprogramming per TSB 21-2244)
Fuse or relay fault in the run/crank feed
Loose or corroded terminal at the module

P2534.d: P2534 is the most widely documented of this group. GM's 2025 tables let the TCM fail it when its run/crank input is false while the ECM reports run/crank active, 99 failures out of 240 samples at 25 ms, Type A; the brake control module (EBCM) sets it when its primary wakeup line reads low for 3 s while the network says run or crank, Type B.
s: MIL on
Stall or no start
Transmission or other modules set follow-up codes
c: Engine harness chafed at a bracket (GM HD trucks, upper control arm bracket)
Module software needing an update (GM 6L50 TCM, Ram eTorque HCP)
Loose terminal on the wakeup line at TCM or BCM

P2535.d: P2535 means the run/crank input stays active while it should be off. GM's 2025 tables fail it in the TCM after 320 of 400 samples with run/crank true while the ECM reports it inactive, Type A, and in the brake control module (EBCM) when the primary wakeup line stays high for 3 s against the network status, Type B; the 2016 Volt uses more than 6.0 V on the line with run/crank inactive.
s: MIL on, code returns at every key-on after clearing
Modules stay awake, battery drain
c: Voltage backfeed from another module (GM K111 fuel pump driver via water-in-fuel sensor circuit)
Run/crank wire touching a battery feed

P2536.d: P2536 is the general fault of the accessory input, the signal that is live when the key or start button is in the accessory position and that on many vehicles also acts as a wake-up line between body and powertrain modules. The code does not say whether the line is open, low or high, only that its state cannot be used.
s: Remote start or key-off functions not working
Accessories behave inconsistently in the accessory position
c: Fault in the accessory feed or wake-up output of the body module
Loose or corroded terminal on the accessory line
Worn accessory contact in the ignition switch

P2537.d: P2537 reports that the accessory or accessory wake-up input sits low where a high level is expected. GM documents it in detail: on the 2016 Volt the ECM fails it when the accessory input is false while the propulsion system has been active for more than 0.5 s; it is a Type B fault over 2 trips, and the 6-speed TCM tables evaluate the same input with no MIL.
s: Remote start inoperative
Power liftgate works only with ignition on
Blower may keep running after engine shutdown (diesel)
c: Open or high-resistance accessory wake-up circuit between BCM and ECM/TCM
Body control module not driving the wake-up output
Poor terminal contact at ECM or TCM connector

P2538.d: P2538 is set when the accessory input reads high in a state where it should be inactive, for instance once the vehicle is switched off and the body module should have released the line. Backfeed from an aftermarket device, a stuck accessory relay or a wire touching a battery feed are the obvious causes.
s: Battery drain while parked
Radio or accessories stay on after key-off
c: Backfeed from aftermarket equipment connected to the accessory line
Accessory wire chafed against a battery feed

P2539.d: P2539 is the general circuit code of the sensor that reports the supply pressure ahead of the high-pressure pump. In VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg it is set once the signal exceeds 4.80 V, which the Passat book attributes to a broken line or contact with the positive supply; below 0.2 V VW stores P2541 instead.
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or reduced power under load
Hard starting, especially after standing
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector not engaged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor or pressure switch
Code logged only in a static self-test without a real fault (Ford Transit 2015)

P253A.d: The PTO sense circuit tells the powertrain modules whether the power take-off is really engaged, usually through a pressure or limit switch on the PTO unit. This feedback matters for OBD: CARB allows makers to suspend affected monitors only while PTO is active and requires readiness to be cleared after 750 minutes of cumulative PTO runtime, and Ford's 2012 summary notes that readiness flags are set to not ready durin
s: PTO status not shown or PTO functions unavailable
Readiness monitors behave unexpectedly
c: Open sense wire or disconnected plug at the PTO unit
Failed PTO pressure or limit switch
PTO feedback configured in the module but no PTO fitted

P253B.d: P253B is not about a broken wire but about a PTO feedback signal that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation. A module can compare the sense input with the operator request, engine speed or transmission state: PTO reported engaged although nobody selected it, or no engagement feedback although the PTO was commanded long enough ago.
s: PTO engagement reported wrongly in the cluster or scan tool
Delayed or failed PTO engagement
Monitors not completing
c: Limit or position switch on the PTO misadjusted
PTO engagement mechanism or clutch sticking
Low air or oil pressure at the PTO engagement and pressure switch

P253C.d: P253C flags a PTO feedback input that reads too low for any valid switch state. Where the sense switch closes to ground on engagement, a grounded wire looks like a permanently engaged PTO; where it pulls up, the same fault hides every engagement.
s: PTO shown as engaged although it is off, or never shown as engaged
Readiness monitors stay incomplete
Possible MIL
c: Sense wire rubbed through to ground near the PTO
Oil or water in the sense switch connector

P253D.d: P253D means the PTO feedback input reads above its valid range. Besides genuine shorts to voltage or an open ground on the sense switch, Ram documents a software cause: bulletin 21-013-15 (replacing 21-005-14) covers 2013–2014 Ram 3500 pickups and 3500, 4500 and 5500 chassis cabs with the 6.7L Cummins and Aisin AS69RC six-speed, where the MIL came on with P253D stored in the transmission module although no defect cou
s: MIL on without a noticeable PTO problem
PTO status wrong in scan data
c: Outdated TCM calibration (Ram heavy-duty with Aisin AS69RC, reflash per bulletin)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground or reference at the PTO sense switch

P253E.d: P253E is stored when the PTO feedback signal flickers between states faster or more often than a real engagement could explain. Vibration on a frame-mounted or transmission-mounted PTO is the classic trigger: a loose terminal, a cracked wire near a bracket or a bouncing switch contact make the signal chatter.
s: PTO indicator flickers
PTO-related idle or shift strategy switches on and off
Readiness monitors keep resetting
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sense switch connector
Wire cracked by vibration near the PTO
Worn sense switch with bouncing contact

P253F.d: P253F states that the engine computer considers the oil used up. Depending on the design this verdict comes from an oil quality sensor or, more often, from an oil life model that tallies operating conditions such as load, temperatures and estimated fuel dilution.
s: Oil change or oil quality warning in the cluster
Remaining oil life shown as zero or dropping unusually fast
c: Oil change overdue, oil actually aged
Oil life counter not reset after the last oil change
Strong fuel dilution from short trips, cold operation or frequent regenerations
Oil life calculation in the engine software too aggressive (update available)

P2540.d: P2540 checks whether the low-pressure fuel sensor's reading is credible. The signal stays inside its electrical window, yet the pressure it reports does not fit what the supply side should be delivering.
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or power loss under load
Long cranking or hard starting
c: Weak in-tank or lift pump causing real pressure deviation
Restricted fuel filter or kinked supply line

P2541.d: P2541 means the signal of the low-pressure fuel sensor is below its valid range - typically a short to ground on the signal line or a lost 5 V sensor supply. VW's 2014 specification books set it below 0.2 V on the Passat, CC and Touareg (VW labels it short to ground, low input or out of range low), whereas a signal above 4.8 V leads to P2539.
s: Check engine light
Hesitation under load
Possible hard starting
c: 5 V reference supply missing or pulled down by another sensor

P2542.d: P2542 means the low-pressure fuel sensor reports a voltage above its permitted range. Deutz is explicit: its MD1 controller stores P2542 when the supply pressure sensor signal rises beyond its normal voltage or is shorted toward the high side (SPN 94, FMI 3), and the EMR system describes P2542-00 as a battery short.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or stalling if real pressure is low
Hard starting
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground wire or pin interrupted
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor with high output

P2543.d: P2543 reports a low-pressure fuel sensor signal with brief interruptions or spikes, although it remains within its electrical range most of the time - a loose pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. Ram names P2543-00 for trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins HO in two PCM software bulletins, 18-013-26 (Ram 2500) and 18-021-25 (Ram 3500), each covering model year 2025 and each listing it next to P254
s: Check engine light, often intermittent
Brief stumbling or hesitation
No symptoms between events
c: Loose or corroded pin at the sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact

P2544.d: P2544 concerns torque requests that another module, usually the transmission control module, sends to the engine module – for example to cut torque during a shift. GM's 2020 table 20OBDG04 checks each TCM message for a wrong protection value (16 of 20), a broken rolling counter (6 of 10), an increase request above 1,298 Nm (6 of 10) or the request type toggling too often (3 of 5), type B with two trips.
s: Check engine light, often with several U-codes
Harsh shifts or reduced engine power
Multiple warning lamps, possibly no-crank
c: Loose or unseated pins at the transmission connector
Data bus disturbance or failing gateway
Transmission module software or internal fault

P2545.d: P2545 means torque request A arrives intact but carries values the receiving module cannot accept as plausible – a requested torque outside the expected window, a request that contradicts the operating state, or one that does not follow up as it should. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table lists P2545 with M, i.e.
s: Check engine light (Ford) or transmission warning
Harsh or delayed shifts
c: Transmission oil leak or incorrect oil level (JLR 9HP48)
Requesting module sends implausible torque values

P2546.d: P2546 says that torque request A, the channel over which one module asks another to raise or cut engine torque, reads below its permitted floor. On a hard-wired request this points to a line pulled toward ground; on a data-bus request it means a value pinned at or under the minimum the receiver accepts.
s: Harsh or delayed gear changes
Transmission warning message or check engine light
Fault often stored together with P2545
c: Oil leak or low oil level in the transmission
Wired request line shorted to ground

P2547.d: P2547 is logged when torque request A sits above the highest value the receiving module will accept. A wired input would read like a line touching a supply voltage or a lost ground at the sender; a bus message would carry an out-of-scale number.
s: Shift-related torque reduction no longer works, firmer shifts
Check engine light depending on make
c: Request line shorted to a supply voltage
Requesting module sends a value above the scale
Poor ground at the requesting module

P2548.d: P2548 is the general fault on a second torque request channel, B, used when a further module besides the transmission may ask the engine for less or more torque. GM spells out who sits on channel B: in the ECM part of its 2017 table 17OBDG04 and again in 19OBDG03A, P2548 checks the traction torque and speed request coming from the electronic brake and traction control module.
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Traction or stability control warning lamp
Reduced traction intervention on slippery roads
c: Data bus disturbance between brake module and engine module
Brake/traction control module sends corrupted messages
Weak battery or poor module power supply

P2549.d: P2549 covers a torque request on channel B that arrives readable but makes no sense: a requested torque outside the expected band, a request that contradicts the current driving state, or one that changes in a way the sender could not plausibly mean. The wiring or bus link is assumed intact here, which separates it from the general fault P2548.
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction control intervenes abruptly or not at all
c: Requesting module (e.g. brake/traction module) computes implausible values
Software levels of sender and engine module do not match
Faulty input data at the requesting module, such as wheel speed

P254A.d: P254A covers the first PTO speed selector: the switch or sensor an operator uses to choose one of the preset working speeds for a power take-off. The engine controller expects a defined signal on this line; with P254A it finds no valid state, typically a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a switch contact that never closes.
s: PTO stays at standby speed instead of the selected step
Selected working speed cannot be called up
Stored code without effect on normal driving
c: Broken selector signal or return wire
Selector or upfitter connector disconnected or pushed-out pin
Switch contact that no longer closes

P254B.d: P254B is the rationality fault of PTO speed selector 1. The wiring is intact and the voltage sits inside the electrical limits, yet the reading does not fit any configured position, or it contradicts other information the controller holds, for example two speed requests at once or a value that lingers between steps.
s: PTO does not leave standby speed
Wrong working speed for the selected position
c: Wrong resistor value in the upfitter's speed coding
Controller configured for a different selector type

P254C.d: P254C reports that the signal from PTO speed selector 1 sits below the lowest voltage the controller accepts, which in practice means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted internally. Whether a maker can detect this at all depends on the design.
s: PTO speed stuck at one step
PTO blocked by the controller
c: Selector signal wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the selector switch
Water in an exterior selector connector

P254D.d: With P254D the controller sees the PTO speed selector 1 input above its upper limit. Causes are a signal wire rubbing against a battery-fed circuit, a broken ground or sensor return that lets the line float to the pull-up voltage, or a selector supply that is too high.
s: PTO jumps to the highest preset speed
PTO does not engage
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Open ground or return line letting the input float high

P254E.d: P254E is set when the signal from PTO speed selector 1 changes faster or more often than a real switch operation can explain, or briefly drops out and returns. Each short glitch can be read as a new speed request, and engine speed then hunts between steps; on Ram chassis cabs with the VSIM interface the controller ramps between the remote presets at 200 rpm per second, so a chattering contact produces audible surging
s: Engine speed surges while the PTO is running
PTO drops briefly to standby speed
Code comes and goes
c: Loose terminal at the selector or upfitter connector
Corroded splice in the upfitter wiring
Vibration on a body-mounted switch panel

P254F.d: P254F concerns the circuit of the hood switch, which tells the control units whether the engine hood is open. Engines that can start on their own, such as in hybrids or stop/start systems, need this to block an automatic start while someone works under the hood.
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Auto-stop or hybrid engine start disabled
Hood-open warning while the hood is closed
c: Hood switch dirty, corroded or misadjusted
Damaged wiring or connector at the hood latch
Bent hood latch after a front-end repair

P2550.d: P2550 marks the second torque request input, B, as stuck below its lower limit. A hard-wired line would be pulled to ground by chafed insulation or a fault in the sending stage; in a networked design the sender would be reporting a value that lies under the bottom of the defined range.
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction-related torque reduction no longer applied
c: Request line chafed through and shorted to ground
Output stage of the requesting module defective

P2551.d: P2551 is the high-side fault of torque request B: the signal sits above the top of its valid window. Typical electrical causes would be a line touching a battery feed, an interrupted reference ground or a sender that drives its output to full scale.
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction control warning, engine ignores intervention requests
c: Request line shorted to battery voltage
Open ground or reference at the sender
Requesting module drives its output to full scale

P2552.d: P2552 is the general circuit fault of throttle/fuel inhibit A, a line over which the engine module can be told, or can itself command, that throttle opening or fuelling must be blocked. It acts as a safety path next to the normal pedal-to-throttle chain.
s: Usually no check engine light (Ford non-MIL)
Possible power limitation or no throttle response
c: Inhibit line open, e.g. broken wire or pushed-out pin
Inhibit relay or its supply defective
Engine module input or output stage faulty

P2553.d: P2553 means the throttle/fuel inhibit path A is electrically present but does not behave as commanded. GM's 2005 diagnostic table for the 3.5 L L66 engine files it under electronic throttle control and runs it as a function check of the inhibit relay over a serial data link: a healthy relay produces no serial data, so any data seen there counts as a failure.
s: Check engine light on the drive after the fault was found
Possible reduced power or throttle limp mode
c: Inhibit relay sticking or contacts worn
Fault in the relay control or feedback wiring
Internal fault in the engine or throttle control unit

P2554.d: P2554 reports that the voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A is too low. In GM's 2005 L66 parameter sheet the limit is below 0.498 V on the analogue inhibit circuit, read by the powertrain module while it is still processing after the ignition has been switched off.
s: Check engine light on the following drive
Sluggish throttle response or reduced power
c: Connected relay or control unit pulls the line down

P2555.d: P2555 indicates excess voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A. The same 2005 GM document for the L66 V6 uses two limits depending on key state: more than 10 V while the ignition is on, or more than 4.5 V once it is off, with the fault judged after 4 s.
s: Check engine light on the next trip
Limited throttle opening or reduced power
c: Inhibit circuit shorted to a battery-fed wire
Missing ground on the receiving side

P2556.d: P2556 is the general circuit code for the coolant level sensor or switch, normally fitted in the expansion tank. Deutz uses it on its EMR L1 engine control for industrial engines with the sub-code P2556-F0, a ground error, under SPN 111.
s: Low coolant warning in the cluster
Coolant level appears correct after opening the cap
c: Damaged wiring or ground at the level sensor
Air cushion in the expansion tank (Mercedes EQB)
Real coolant loss, e.g. internal charge air cooler leak

P2557.d: P2557 means the coolant level signal is electrically present but not believable. The Deutz EMR L1 engine control is the one documented user and fills the code twice under SPN 111: P2557-00 for a sensor value outside the valid range, and P2557-1C when the supply voltage feeding the level sensor is itself out of range.
s: Coolant level warning appears and disappears
Engine protection warning on industrial engines
c: Sensor supply voltage out of range (Deutz P2557-1C)
Level sensor element contaminated or failing
Air pocket or foam in the expansion tank distorting the reading

P2558.d: P2558 reports that the coolant level sensor or switch signal sits too low on the electrical scale. Deutz assigns it on the EMR L1 controller as P2558-14 under SPN 111 and groups two causes together: a grounded line or an interrupted one, which on that input both pull the reading to the bottom.
s: Permanent low coolant warning despite a full tank
No warning possible if the level really drops
c: Broken wire or corroded connector at the expansion tank

P2559.d: P2559 is the high-voltage fault in the circuit of the coolant level sensor or switch. In the Deutz EMR L1 code list it appears as P2559-12 under SPN 111 meaning the line is shorted to battery plus; Deutz keeps open circuits under P2558 on that input, so a high reading there really points to contact with a positive feed.
s: Low coolant warning does not work
Warning lamp or message for the level sensor
c: Signal line chafed against a positive feed
Open circuit on pull-up type switch designs

P255A.d: P255A belongs to the second PTO speed selector input, which lets the operator call up a further preset working speed in addition to selector 1. The controller finds no valid state on this line: a wire is broken, a connector is off, or the switch contact never closes.
s: Second preset speed unavailable
Selector 1 presets still work
c: Broken wire between selector 2 and the module
Upfitter connector for selector 2 not mated

P255B.d: P255B flags an implausible reading from PTO speed selector 2 although its circuit is electrically intact. Because a second selector normally works together with the first, the check can compare both: requests that cannot coexist, a level that sits between valid positions, or a selection that the configured number of presets does not allow.
s: Second preset ignored or wrong speed reached
PTO speed control falls back to standby
c: Upfitter wiring ties selector 1 and 2 together
Number of programmed presets does not match the switch

P255C.d: P255C means the input of PTO speed selector 2 reads lower than the controller's bottom limit, usually because the signal wire has a short to chassis ground or the switch is shorted inside. On designs where a grounded line is itself the command, as with the switch-to-ground inputs of Ram's 2017 VSIM, a short looks exactly like a permanently held preset 2 request; the controller can only tell the difference when the se
s: Engine always runs at the second preset in PTO mode
PTO blocked
c: Selector 2 wire shorted to chassis ground
Harness pinched under a body mounting

P255D.d: P255D is stored when PTO speed selector 2 delivers a signal above the permitted maximum. A chafed wire touching a battery-fed circuit, a lost sensor ground, or an upfitter feeding 12 V into an input meant to be switched to ground are the realistic causes.
s: Second preset unavailable
PTO switched off by the controller
c: Selector 2 wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Upfitter applies 12 V to a ground-switched input
Lost ground or return line of selector 2

P255E.d: P255E concerns short dropouts or rapid changes on the PTO speed selector 2 signal that do not match deliberate operation. Selector 2 is often the remote control on the body, close to pumps, booms or spreaders, so vibration, spray water and cable movement hit it harder than an in-cab switch.
s: Engine steps through preset speeds unexpectedly
PTO speed unstable while working
Code appears only under vibration
c: Spray water or moisture in the body-mounted remote switch
Cable to the remote control flexing at a boom or hinge
Loose crimp or terminal in the selector 2 circuit

P255F.d: P255F flags the A/C request A input as electrically sound but implausible: the request may switch on and off far more often than a real compressor demand would, stay set while the climate control is off, or disagree with what the engine module sees from the compressor side. The request lets the engine prepare for the compressor load by raising idle speed and torque reserve.
s: Idle speed fluctuates when the A/C cycles
A/C cooling intermittent or switched off
c: Climate control module sends erratic requests
Loose contact on the request line causing chatter

P2560.d: P2560 is not an electrical fault but a level finding: the coolant level sensor works, yet it reports less coolant than the minimum. Deutz uses it on the EMR L1 control as P2560-00 under SPN 111 with failure mode 1, meaning the level has fallen under its warning threshold.
s: Low coolant warning
Rising engine temperature or overheating
Visible coolant traces or sweet smell
c: External leak at hoses, radiator or water pump
Internal leak, e.g. charge air cooler or head gasket
Air trapped after a coolant service

P2561.d: P2561 is a messenger code. The climate control module has found an emission-relevant fault in its own area, such as a component that feeds the engine's A/C idle strategy, and asks the engine module to switch on the warning lamp, since only the master controller may drive it.
s: Check engine light on
A/C may not cool or may be switched off
Further codes stored in the climate control module
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the climate control module
Failed A/C sensor or actuator behind that fault
Climate control module internal or software fault

P2562.d: P2562 flags a general electrical problem in the circuit of the position sensor that reports where turbocharger boost actuator A stands - the variable vane linkage on many diesels, the electric wastegate actuator on turbo petrol engines. The engine computer receives a signal it cannot use at all, as opposed to a wrong position (P2563), a signal pinned low or high (P2564/P2565) or brief dropouts (P2566).
s: Reduced power because boost is limited
Check engine light on
P2565 stored at the same time on some engines
c: Open or corroded wiring or connector between position sensor and engine computer
Electronic wastegate actuator rod length out of adjustment
Position sensor inside the actuator failed

P2563.d: P2563 means the position feedback of the turbocharger boost control actuator - variable vanes or wastegate - does not match the commanded position, without an open or short being reported. GM's 2009 Duramax diesel table sets it when vane position differs from target by 15 % or more for 5 s (Type B, warning light after two trips).
s: Noticeable loss of power, limp mode
Check engine light
Underboost code P0299 stored at the same time
c: Kinked, twisted or leaking vacuum hose to the boost actuator
Leaking actuator diaphragm or sticking vanes
Broken or missing adjustment stud, actuator travel out of tolerance

P2564.d: P2564 is stored when the voltage from the boost actuator position sensor stays below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver, which usually points to a short to ground or a lost reference supply. GM's 2009 Duramax table uses 0.277 V (5.5 %, vanes fully open) held for 1 s once the engine has run 3 s, Type B.
s: Noticeable loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light on
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground near the turbocharger
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing or shorted
Failed position sensor or vane actuator

P2565.d: P2565 means the boost actuator position signal sits above the highest plausible value, typically from an open signal wire, a short to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor. GM's 2018 diesel ECM table flags it at an analog reading above 95 % in 200 of 250 samples (Type A, warning lamp on the first trip).
s: Loss of power, sometimes limp mode
Check engine light on
Unusual turbocharger noise on some diesels
c: Open signal wire or unplugged actuator connector
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Wastegate actuator rod set to the wrong length (electric wastegate engines)
Failed vane actuator with integrated sensor

P2566.d: P2566 reports that the signal from the boost control position sensor flickers or drops out briefly instead of being steadily wrong. VW bulletins 21-15-04 (2015) and 21-15-06 (2020) for 2009-2014 Jetta, Golf and Jetta SportWagen with the 2.0 L TDI (CBEA, CJAA) list P2566 together with P2562-P2565 and P0299 for the complaint of lacking power; there the position sensor G581 sits in the vacuum diaphragm, and the repair p
s: Intermittent loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light, sometimes going out again
Surging boost
c: Loose or corroded pin at the position sensor connector
Heat-damaged or chafed sensor wiring near the turbocharger
Worn position sensor in the actuator

P2567.d: P2567 is the general circuit fault of the sensor fitted to a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator - a radiator with a catalytic coating that converts ground-level ozone in the passing air and earns low-emission vehicles an NMOG credit. CARB section (e)(14) requires the OBD system to detect a missing or deteriorated DOR function.
s: Check engine light
No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection because of the stored code
c: Damaged sensor wiring or connector at the radiator
Replacement radiator without coating or without sensor fitted

P2568.d: P2568 is the plausibility check of the sensor on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator, whose coating converts ozone in the cooling air. VW's 2014 specification books for the CC and Tiguan set it on a failed ID check or a failed functional check of the temperature sensor.
s: Check engine light, often after a radiator replacement
No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection
c: Aftermarket radiator without ozone coating or without the identification sensor
Identification sensor not bonded after radiator replacement

P2569.d: P2569 means the radiator-mounted sensor of a DOR system (direct ozone reduction: a radiator coating that breaks down ozone in the incoming air) shows an electrical fault toward ground. According to VW's 2014 data books for the CC with 2.0 L TSI (CBFA, CCTA) and the Tiguan (CCTA), the sensor talks to the engine computer over a LIN line, and P2569 is set when that link fails because the line is grounded.
s: Check engine light on
No change in driveability or engine temperature
Emissions inspection may be refused
c: LIN wire to the radiator sensor chafed and shorted to ground
Water or salt corrosion in the radiator sensor connector
Internal short in the radiator sensor

P256A.d: P256A refers to the switch or sensor with which the driver chooses a raised idle speed, for example to run a generator, an inverter or belt-driven equipment while parked, independent of any PTO. The controller sees no valid state on this input, which points to an open wire, a disconnected plug or a switch that no longer makes contact.
s: Raised idle cannot be selected
Engine stays at normal idle
c: Open wire in the idle selector circuit
Selector connector loose or not mated

P256B.d: P256B means the idle speed selector delivers a value that is electrically valid but makes no sense in context. The controller may, for instance, see a raised-idle request with the truck in motion, a position that does not exist, or a request that conflicts with an active PTO mode; Ram's 2012 chassis cab guide states that remote PTO outranks the Idle Up function, so the two inputs have a defined order the software can
s: Raised idle request ignored
Idle selection works only sometimes
c: Aftermarket idle control wired into the same circuit
Idle or PTO configuration changed without matching hardware

P256C.d: P256C says the idle speed selector input is pulled below its lowest valid level, typically by a signal wire shorted to ground or a switch with an internal short. Where the selector is a simple ground-switched input, the controller would read such a short as a permanent request, so a dedicated low code presupposes a coded or monitored circuit.
s: Raised idle unavailable
Code returns after every key cycle
c: Idle selector wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the idle selector

P256D.d: P256D is logged when the idle speed selector signal rises above the highest value the controller treats as valid. Causes include a wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit, an open sensor return that lets the input float high, or an accessory module that drives the line with system voltage.
s: Raised idle cannot be selected
Normal driving unaffected
c: Selector wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Open return line letting the input float high
Accessory module feeding system voltage into the line

P256E.d: P256E records an idle speed selector signal that drops out or flickers for short moments, more often than real switch use would cause. Since the selector is usually operated with the engine idling for long periods, engine vibration, a worn rocker switch or a loose crimp can be enough; each interruption can cancel the raised idle and make the engine fall back and rise again.
s: Raised idle drops out and comes back
Engine speed rises and falls at standstill
Code stored only intermittently
c: Loose crimp or terminal in the selector circuit
Harness moving with engine vibration at idle

P256F.d: P256F is the plausibility fault of a second A/C request input, B. Its wiring checks out, yet the engine module finds the state or timing illogical, for instance a request present while the first input and the climate controller say no cooling is wanted, or one that flickers instead of holding steady.
s: Rear or second-stage cooling unreliable
Idle dips or surges with A/C operation
c: Climate control logic sends inconsistent B request
Intermittent connection on the B request line
Fault in a second evaporator or compressor stage control

P2570.d: P2570 is the high-side electrical fault of the sensor fitted to a DOR radiator, the ozone-converting coated radiator found on some low-emission petrol cars. VW's 2014 Tiguan book (2.0 L TSI, CCTA) logs it when LIN communication with the sensor breaks down because the line is interrupted or carries battery voltage; the 2014 CC book applies the same criterion to its CBFA and CCTA engines.
s: Check engine light, often right after radiator work
Engine runs and cools normally
c: Sensor not connected or not fitted after radiator replacement
Broken LIN wire or loose terminal

P2571.d: P2571 stands for an unsteady or intermittently lost signal from the temperature sensor of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst. Unlike P2569 and P2570, which describe a lasting low or high fault, this code covers readings that jump around or vanish for moments.
s: Check engine light that may come and go
No noticeable effect on driving or cooling
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the radiator sensor plug
Sensor no longer firmly bonded to the radiator
Harness damaged by vibration at the radiator mounting

P2572.d: P2572 points to a general fault in the circuit of a sensor meant to judge how much ozone-converting activity is left on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst, such as a coated radiator. CARB demands a real deterioration check only when the DOR credit is above 5 mg/mi NMOG on LEV III/IV vehicles (or half the NMOG standard on older ones); at or below that, the system merely has to notice a total loss of ozone reducti
s: Check engine light on
No effect on engine power or cooling
c: Damaged wiring or connector at the DOR sensor
Replacement radiator without the sensor fitted

P2573.d: P2573 means the deterioration sensor watching a DOR (direct ozone reduction) catalyst delivers a signal that is electrically within limits but does not fit the expected behaviour, for example a value that never changes with conditions or contradicts other inputs. Such a sensor would estimate how much of the catalytic coating on the radiator still destroys ozone, which CARB requires on vehicles claiming a large DOR cr
s: Check engine light after several drive cycles
No change in how the car drives
c: Deterioration sensor drifting or stuck at one value
Non-original radiator with a sensor that does not match
Radiator face heavily fouled, skewing the sensor reading

P2574.d: P2574 is set when the deterioration sensor circuit of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst reads below its valid range, the usual signature of a short to ground or a failed sensor pulling the line down. No manufacturer documents P2574 publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Car drives and cools as before
c: Sensor wire shorted to ground at the radiator

P2575.d: P2575 reports a deterioration-sensor signal above the valid range on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - typical for an open circuit, a missing ground or a short to a supply voltage. No vehicle maker has published how it uses P2575, and no service bulletin naming it turned up in the NHTSA index.
s: Check engine light on
No change in power or engine temperature
c: Connector left off or damaged during radiator work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P2576.d: P2576 describes a deterioration-sensor signal on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst that comes and goes or jumps without a physical reason, rather than staying low (P2574) or high (P2575). Loose terminals, a cracked connector housing in the airstream ahead of the engine, or chafing where the harness meets the radiator are typical suspects, since that spot sees vibration, spray water and road salt.
s: Check engine light, possibly only now and then
No noticeable driving symptoms
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing at the radiator support
Cracked connector housing letting water in

P2577.d: P2577 means the OBD system has concluded that the direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - usually a radiator coated with an ozone-destroying catalyst such as BASF's PremAir - no longer converts enough ozone. CARB ties the threshold to the credit claimed: for LEV III/IV vehicles with a DOR credit of 5 mg/mi NMOG or less, a malfunction is a system with no measurable ozone reduction left; above 5 mg/mi, it is a performa
s: Check engine light on
No change in engine cooling or performance
Possible failed emissions inspection
c: Catalytic coating worn, damaged or covered with dirt
Faulty DOR sensor giving a false result

P2578.d: P2578 is the catch-all electrical fault for speed sensor A, the pickup that counts revolutions of the turbocharger or supercharger shaft, normally by sensing a tone feature on the compressor wheel or its nut. The engine computer logs it when the sensor line is faulty in a way it cannot classify as too low, too high or sporadic; those cases have their own codes P2580, P2581 and P2582, and P2579 covers a readable but i
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because boost is limited as a precaution
Turbo speed missing or frozen in live data
c: Loose, corroded or oil-soaked connector at the speed sensor
Harness chafed or heat-damaged near the hot turbocharger housing
Internal failure of speed sensor A
Fault in the engine control module input stage

P2579.d: P2579 means speed sensor A delivers a signal, but the shaft speed it reports does not fit the operating state the engine computer expects from boost, airflow and load. PACCAR bulletin E209 for 2017-2019 MX-11 and MX-13 truck engines treats P2579, alone or with P1581, as a fix-as-fail item: the sensor is replaced, because it tends to fail intermittently with a loss of power that disappears when the driver lifts off an
s: Sudden loss of power that returns after lifting off the accelerator
Malfunction indicator lamp on
Turbo speed in live data jumping or inconsistent with boost
c: Speed sensor A dropping out intermittently
Engine software that misjudges the speed plausibility (update available on some models)
Intake or boost leak that makes the shaft speed differ from the model
Mechanical turbocharger problem such as bearing drag or wheel damage

P257A.d: P257A is an output fault on the control line of the vacuum reservoir, usually a solenoid or switching valve the engine computer uses to connect, isolate or vent a vacuum storage tank. Such tanks occur mainly on diesels whose EGR valves, turbocharger vanes or flaps are worked by vacuum; GM bulletin PI1260 for the 2014 Cruze 2.0 L diesel, for example, shows the pump filling a tank built into the EGR cooler, which in tu
s: Engine warning lamp on
Vacuum-driven actuators such as EGR or turbo vanes respond poorly
c: Loose or corroded connector at the reservoir control valve
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Open solenoid coil in the control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P257B.d: P257B points to a vacuum reservoir control circuit whose voltage is too low, which in practice usually means a ground short on the line between the control unit and the reservoir valve, or a driver stage that cannot hold the line at its proper level. The valve manages a vacuum store used by pneumatic actuators such as EGR valves or turbocharger vanes, mostly on diesel engines.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Follow-up codes for EGR or turbocharger position
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the reservoir control valve
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P257C.d: P257C sets when the control line of the vacuum reservoir valve reads too high, typically from a short to battery positive or a fault in the driver stage, so the valve can no longer be switched as commanded. The reservoir serves pneumatic actuators on diesel engines; GM's bulletin PI1260 on the 2014 Cruze diesel names leaks anywhere in the vacuum system that feeds the turbo vane and EGR actuators as a cause of P003A,
s: Engine warning lamp on
Weaker boost or EGR response in some cases
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Internal fault in the reservoir control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P257D.d: P257D is the plausibility fault of the engine hood switch. The line is electrically readable, but the value falls into a band the module regards as impossible, or two redundant switches disagree.
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Hood ajar message although the hood is closed
Auto stop-start or remote start not available
c: Hood switch or plunger worn, misadjusted or contaminated
Fluid or corrosion in the switch or ECM connector shunting the signal
Second hood switch or latch switch reporting a different state
Replacement switch with wrong resistance coding

P257E.d: P257E says the hood switch signal has dropped below its lowest valid level, which usually means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted inside. GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 sets it for a resistance-coded switch at 325 ohms or less, the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 at 14.6 % of range or less, each with 80 failures in 100 samples and Type B.
s: Hood ajar indicator on with the hood shut
Engine stop-start inoperative
Check engine lamp on
c: Hood switch signal wire chafed to ground near the latch
Hood switch and horn connectors swapped after front-end repair
Switch shorted internally by water or impact damage

P257F.d: P257F is the high-side counterpart of P257E: the hood switch reading rises above the top limit, which points to an open signal line, a pin that has backed out of its connector, or a short to a voltage source. In GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 the limit for a resistance-coded switch is 3,620 ohms or more, and the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 uses 71.5 % of range; both need 80 failures within 100 samples and are Type B
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stop-start stays inactive
Hood warning may be shown or may be missing when the hood is really open
c: Open hood switch signal wire or unplugged switch
Loose or pushed-back pins in a front harness connector
Signal line shorted to a voltage source

P2580.d: P2580 says the signal from turbocharger or supercharger speed sensor A stays at the low end, so the engine computer sees too little or no usable pulse activity - typically from a short to ground, a weak sensor or a pickup that cannot read the target. A Stellantis STAR case from November 2023 for 2022-2024 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks reports P2580 with the warning lamp, sometimes after few miles; besides the normal circui
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Turbo speed reads zero or very low in live data
Possible boost limitation and reduced power
c: Debris on the tone wheel or an extra O-ring in the sensor bore
Speed sensor A with weak or missing output

P2581.d: P2581 is set when speed sensor A reports a level above what a healthy circuit can produce, so the engine computer cannot trust it. Typical triggers are a signal wire shorted to the supply or battery voltage, an open signal or ground path that lets the input float high, or a sensor with a shorted output stage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high or fixed turbo speed in live data
Reduced boost and power
c: Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open ground or signal wire letting the input float high
Speed sensor A with a shorted output

P2582.d: P2582 points to a speed sensor A signal that cuts out or jumps for short moments while being fine in between, so the fault may be gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop. Loose terminals, a cracked wire that opens under vibration or heat, and a sensor failing internally when hot are the usual suspects.
s: Brief power dips that come and go
Warning lamp that may switch off again
Turbo speed trace with dropouts or spikes
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire break that opens only under vibration or heat
Speed sensor A failing when hot

P2583.d: P2583 points to the front distance sensor of adaptive cruise control – the only radar, or the centre unit where several are fitted. The engine module keeps the code because adaptive cruise acts directly on engine torque.
s: Adaptive cruise control switches off or cannot be engaged
Warning to clean the radar sensor
Collision mitigation braking unavailable, warning lamps on
c: Snow, ice, dirt or a non-approved grille trim in front of the radar
Radar software needing the manufacturer update
Radar misaligned after a knock or bumper repair
Radar unit or its wiring faulty

P2584.d: P2584 belongs to diesel cars that add a fuel-borne catalyst to the tank so the particulate filter can burn off soot at lower exhaust temperatures. A separate additive module meters the fluid after each refuelling, in proportion to fuel added, and watches its pump, level sensor and its own circuits.
s: Check engine lamp on
Particulate filter warning, regenerations incomplete
Loss of power as soot load rises
c: Additive reservoir empty or level sensor faulty
Additive dosing pump or injector failed
Additive module wiring, supply or CAN link faulty
Additive quantity counter not reset after refill or filter change

P2585.d: P2585 is the softer sibling of P2584. Here the fuel additive module asks for a warning lamp other than the MIL – typically a service or particulate filter indicator – because something needs attention before emissions suffer.
s: Service or particulate filter warning lamp on
Message about additive level in the instrument cluster
c: Refill or new additive bag not registered with the scan tool
Level sensor in the additive reservoir faulty

P2586.d: P2586 covers a general electrical fault at position sensor B, which reports where the second boost control actuator stands - the vane mechanism or electric wastegate of a second turbocharger on engines that regulate two of them separately. The engine computer cannot use the feedback, without the fault being pinned down as low (P2588), high (P2589) or sporadic (P2590); P2587 is a position mismatch with a working circu
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because boost is capped
No valid position value for actuator B in live data
c: Connector or terminal fault at the actuator B position sensor
Harness to actuator B damaged by exhaust heat
Position sensor inside actuator B failed (often replaced as a unit)

P2587.d: P2587 is a plausibility fault: position sensor B gives an electrically valid reading, but the reported position of the second boost actuator does not follow the command, or the value lies outside what the mechanism can physically reach. No manufacturer documents P2587 publicly, so the logic is known only from sensor A.
s: Noticeable loss of power or overboost cut
Malfunction indicator lamp on
Commanded and actual position of actuator B diverge in live data
c: Sticking variable vanes or wastegate linkage on turbo B
Kinked or leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on pneumatic actuators
Actuator rod or adjusting stud out of adjustment or broken

P2588.d: P2588 is stored when the voltage from position sensor B of the second boost actuator drops below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver - most often a grounded signal line or a missing 5 V reference. No manufacturer documents P2588 publicly; the thresholds known for sensor A give the order of magnitude.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Power reduced, boost held low
Further sensor codes if a shared reference is shorted
c: Signal wire of position sensor B shorted to ground
Lost or shorted 5 V reference supply
Failed position sensor B in actuator B

P2589.d: P2589 means the signal that position sensor B returns for the second boost actuator sits above its plausible maximum, typically from an open signal or ground wire, a short to the reference or battery voltage, or a sensor with a defective output. No manufacturer documents P2589 publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often on the first trip
Reduced power with boost capped
Position of actuator B stuck near the maximum in live data
c: Open signal or ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Wastegate rod set so the sensor reads at its upper end

P258A.d: P258A stands for an open or otherwise faulty control circuit A of an electric vacuum pump, which supplies the brake booster on engines that provide too little manifold vacuum, such as hybrids, downsized turbo petrol engines and diesels. Ford's 2018-2019 hybrid OBD summary assigns it to the brake system module: with the pump relay commanded off, a monitoring line voltage outside 1.3-5.0 V for 100 ms sets the code (leg
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
Harder brake pedal at low speed or after several stops
Start-stop function disabled
c: False entry after a long engine crank while the pump is unpowered
Faulty pump relay, blown fuse or poor relay contact
Open wire or loose connector between module, relay and pump

P258B.d: P258B is the range/performance code for control circuit A of the vacuum pump: the pump is commanded, but its monitoring feedback or the vacuum it produces does not fit. Ford's 2018-2019 hybrid OBD summary sets it from the brake module when the monitoring line sits outside 1.3-5.0 V with the relay off, or below 250 mV for 1 s with the relay on.
s: Engine, brake or stability warning lamp on
Hard brake pedal, less brake assist
Start-stop fault message
c: Worn or failed electric vacuum pump
Leaking hose or check valve that makes the pump run too long
Blown pump fuse, spread terminals or poor ground
Outdated engine software controlling pump duty cycle

P258C.d: P258C reports that control circuit A of the electrically driven vacuum pump reads too low, typically because the control or relay line is shorted to ground, the relay coil is faulty, or a blown supply fuse leaves the monitoring line without voltage. Depending on how the circuit is laid out, the pump may then run nonstop or not at all.
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
Pump silent or running constantly
Firmer brake pedal
c: Control or relay wire shorted to ground
Faulty pump relay or relay coil

P258D.d: P258D marks a control circuit A of the vacuum pump whose signal sits above the expected range, most often a short to battery positive on the relay or pump control line, so the control unit can no longer switch the pump as it wants. If the pump keeps running, it wears out early; FCA case S1805000006 notes that pumps forced into excessive run time tend to fail.
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
