Vacuum pump runs continuously, even with the engine off in some cases
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P258E.d: P258E is the plausibility check of the power take-off enable switch. The line is not open or shorted – those faults are P251A to P251C – but the state of the switch does not fit the other PTO inputs, for instance an enable request without a valid arming step or contact signals that contradict each other.
s: PTO cannot be switched on or switches off unexpectedly
Driver information message about PTO conditions
c: PTO switch contacts worn or contaminated, mode signals disagree
Upfitter wiring or load-engage switch interfering with the enable input
Remote enable used without arming sequence or with wrong switch type
PTO module configuration not matching the installed switches

P258F.d: P258F concerns the sending side of a torque management link. One controller – for example the engine module talking to a transmission or hybrid controller, or the reverse – transmits torque requests and finds that its own output is faulty, missing or not accepted by the receiver.
s: Check engine lamp on
Harsh or delayed shifts
Reduced engine power
c: CAN wiring or connector fault between the modules
Software levels of sending and receiving module do not match
Low voltage or poor ground at one of the modules

P2590.d: P2590 is set when the position signal of the second boost actuator flickers, jumps or drops out for short moments instead of being steadily wrong. Unlike its sensor A counterpart P2566, this code is defined as intermittent/erratic, so an unsteady signal without full dropouts falls under it as well.
s: Power surging or dropping intermittently
Warning lamp that may come and go
Jumping position value for actuator B in live data
c: Loose terminal or intermittent contact in the sensor B connector
Sensor track worn by vibration, giving a noisy signal
Chafed harness that shorts or opens briefly

P2591.d: P2591 is reserved for the left front distance sensor in cruise systems that combine several radars across the front; a single or centre unit uses P2583 and the right one P2592. No manufacturer documents P2591 publicly.
s: Adaptive cruise control not available
Driver assistance warning message
c: Bumper cover damaged, replaced or repainted over the left sensor
Left sensor bracket bent, sensor aimed wrongly
Ice, mud or stickers covering the sensor area
Sensor or wiring to the left corner faulty

P2592.d: P2592 marks a fault of the right-hand front distance sensor in multi-radar adaptive cruise layouts; the left unit reports P2591, a single or centre radar P2583. No maker publishes this code.
s: Adaptive cruise control switched off
Warning message for the radar or driver assistance system
c: Right sensor knocked out of alignment by kerb or parking contact
Road salt or water corrosion at the right sensor connector
Sensor not recalibrated after bumper replacement

P2593.d: P2593 concerns the second turbocharger speed sensor, found where an engine has two turbochargers, for example one per cylinder bank. It marks an electrical fault on that sensor's circuit that is not further classified; the specific forms are P2595 (low), P2596 (high) and P2597 (intermittent), while P2594 covers a plausibility error.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Power reduced, often only slightly with one turbo affected
No speed value for the second turbo in live data
c: Connector problem at speed sensor B
Harness to the second turbocharger damaged by heat or chafing
Internal failure of speed sensor B

P2594.d: P2594 means the second turbocharger speed sensor produces a signal, but its reported speed does not agree with what the engine computer predicts for that turbo. Bentley documents it on the W12 in the Continental GT/GTC, Flying Spur and Bentayga (bulletin 2053348, versions 5 and 10): after a smoke test of intake and exhaust, a detached divider inside the air filter box on Continental and Flying Spur turned out to be o
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fault often appears only under particular load or gradient conditions
Turbo speeds of both banks differ noticeably in live data
c: Detached divider in the air filter box disturbing the flow to one turbo
Intake or exhaust leak on the bank of the second turbo
Speed sensor B delivering an implausible signal

P2595.d: P2595 is logged when the signal of turbocharger speed sensor B stays below the range the engine computer accepts, as with a short to ground or a sensor whose output has collapsed. Bentley names it for the W12 in Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur from 2018 and later also in the Bentayga, stored in engine control unit 1 or 2.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Speed of the second turbo shown as zero or very low
Possible reduction of boost
c: Speed sensor B with collapsed output
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Corroded or contaminated connector at sensor B

P2596.d: With P2596 the engine computer sees the line of turbocharger speed sensor B sitting above its valid window - the usual pattern for a signal shorted to supply voltage, an interrupted ground or a defective sensor output. The code was added to Bentley's W12 speed-sensor bulletin in its later revision (2053348/10, December 2022), which also brought in the Bentayga; it is handled like the low fault: work through the wirin
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high speed for the second turbo in live data
Possible boost reduction
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Defective output stage of speed sensor B

P2597.d: P2597 records short interruptions or jumps in the signal of the second turbocharger speed sensor, between which the circuit works normally. Such faults usually sit in a connector, a wire that breaks contact under engine movement or heat soak, or a sensor that drops out when hot.
s: Occasional warning lamp, sometimes only after long drives
Short power dips under load
Dropouts in the speed trace of the second turbo
c: Loose terminal or poor pin contact at sensor B
Wire breaking contact under engine movement or heat soak
Speed sensor B dropping out when hot

P2598.d: P2598 means the boost control position of turbocharger A, normally the vane or wastegate position reported by the actuator, appears stuck toward its low end: the measured value no longer follows the command although the signal is electrically valid. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary runs this check with closed-loop position control active above 500 rpm and flags a gap of more than 15 % in either direction lasting 25 s,
s: Engine warning lamp on
Lack of power under load, boost limited
Unusual turbo noise
c: Sooted or seized variable vanes that no longer follow the actuator
Vacuum leak or kinked hose on pneumatically driven actuators
Worn or failed electric vane actuator
One-off entry from unusual operation, e.g. after delivery transport

P2599.d: P2599 is the high-side stuck fault for position sensor A: the turbocharger actuator stays at, or reports, a position beyond where it should be, while the sensor circuit itself works. GM documents it twice.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Overboost cut-out or noticeable power reduction
Black smoke or rough response under load
c: Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position by soot or corrosion
Weak return spring or binding linkage that keeps the actuator from its rest position
Vacuum control solenoid or hose fault on pneumatic actuators
Defective actuator electronics on smart actuators

P259A.d: P259A applies to engines with a second boost control actuator, for instance a twin-turbo layout or the second stage of a two-stage system, whose position is read by sensor B. The code is stored when that actuator's reported position stays at the low end and stops tracking the command even though the signal is electrically sound.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Weak acceleration, notably in the range where charger B works
c: Sticking vanes, flap or wastegate on charger B
Weak vacuum or electrical supply to actuator B
Worn actuator B or misadjusted linkage

P259B.d: P259B is logged when the boost control actuator watched by position sensor B is found stuck at the high end of its travel, or fails to return to its rest position, while the sensor signal itself is plausible. A sensor B exists mainly on twin-turbo or two-stage engines.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Power cut-out under full load to prevent overboost
c: Mechanism of charger B seized toward the closed or high position
Return spring or linkage of actuator B binding
Vacuum solenoid or hose of actuator B faulty (pneumatic systems)

P259C.d: P259C reports that closed-loop boost control of turbocharger A was not reached within the expected time after its enabling conditions were met. Instead of trimming the actuator from boost or position feedback, the controller stays in open-loop or default mode.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Sluggish or uneven boost build-up
c: Boost pressure or actuator position sensor fault that blocks closed-loop control
Actuator A fault, often with its own stored code
Charge air leak preventing boost from reaching the range where control starts

P259D.d: P259D is the turbocharger B version of the closed-loop timing fault. On engines with two separately regulated chargers, the control unit expects the boost regulation of the second unit to switch to feedback operation within a set time, and here it did not.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Reduced power, especially at higher load
c: Fault on position or pressure sensing for charger B
Actuator B or its control circuit faulty
Leak in the charge air path of charger B

P259E.d: P259E means the boost control of turbocharger A has run out of range at the low end: the actuator is at its limit, yet boost stays well under the target. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary places it in the underboost monitor.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Clear loss of power under load
Whistling or hissing from the charge air side
c: Leak in charge air pipes, intercooler or clamps
Variable vane actuator or vane mechanism not reaching the commanded position
Exhaust leak upstream of the turbine
Boost pressure sensor reading too low

P259F.d: P259F is the counterpart of P259E: the regulation of turbocharger A has hit its upper limit, and measured boost runs above the value the engine computer asked for. In Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary it is the overboost monitor, checked continuously between 800 (6.7 L) or 1300 rpm (3.0 L) and 4000 rpm with at least 50 or 135 Nm of torque; it sets when actual boost exceeds the target by more than 120 kPa on the 6.7 L or
s: Engine warning lamp on
Sudden power cut at high load
c: Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position
Actuator or its vacuum/electrical control not opening as commanded
Engine control software needing an update
Boost pressure sensor reading too high

P25A0.d: P25A0 says the regulator of turbocharger B has run to its low limit without reaching the boost target, so the second charger delivers too little pressure even with full control authority. It only exists on engines where two chargers are regulated separately.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Lower power than usual, uneven pull
c: Leak in the charge air path served by charger B
Wastegate or vanes of charger B not closing as commanded

P25A1.d: P25A1 is set when the boost control for turbocharger B is pinned at its upper limit and still cannot bring pressure down to the requested value, so the second charger overshoots. Like P25A0 it is limited to engines with two individually controlled chargers, and no manufacturer has published its own criteria for P25A1.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Power cut-out at high load
c: Wastegate or vanes of charger B stuck toward closed
Blocked, leaking or misrouted control line of actuator B
Boost pressure sensor giving wrong values

P25A2.d: P25A2 is a messenger code: the brake system control module has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to light the check engine lamp. GM's 2017 engine table 17OBDG04 and 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 watch this request continuously from three seconds after power-up and class the engine module entry itself as Type A without a separate lamp request, because the lamp is already on the brake
s: Check engine lamp on
ABS, stability or driver assistance warnings at the same time
Brake pedal may feel soft in some cases
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the brake control module
Weak battery or low system voltage upsetting the brake module
Brake or related module software needing an update
Lost communication with a partner module such as the front camera

P25A3.d: P25A3 is a state code, not a wiring fault: the hood is reported open at a moment when the control strategy expects it closed, for example while an automatic restart, a remote start or a hybrid engine pull-up is pending. No manufacturer documents P25A3 publicly.
s: Hood open warning in the cluster
Auto stop-start and remote start locked out
Engine keeps running at standstill instead of stopping
c: Hood only on the safety catch, not fully latched
Hood switch or striker misadjusted after body work
Latch-integrated switch sticking in the open position

P25A4.d: P25A4 is the general circuit fault for the fuel mode select switch – the button on bi-fuel vehicles with which the driver chooses between gasoline and an alternative fuel such as CNG or LPG. GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala, described in PI1330, has it on the instrument panel left of the steering wheel; on the 2016 Silverado and Sierra 2500HD CNG trucks it sits in the centre stack and carries the fuel indicator.
s: Fuel cannot be changed with the switch
Engine runs on gasoline only
Fuel indicator light on the switch dark or flashing
c: Open wire or unplugged connector at the fuel mode switch
Faulty connection in a bi-fuel conversion harness

P25A5.d: P25A5 flags a performance problem with the fuel mode select switch. The circuit is electrically sound, yet the switch behaves in a way that cannot be genuine, such as a momentary button that appears to be held down for minutes or a press that never returns to rest.
s: Fuel mode changes by itself or not at all
Switch indicator keeps flashing
c: Switch button sticking or contaminated by liquid
Panel trim pressing on the switch after installation work
Replacement switch of the wrong type or coding

P25A6.d: P25A6 means the fuel mode select switch signal has fallen below the range the module accepts. On a switch that pulls a reference line towards ground when pressed, this is the signature of a signal wire rubbed through to the body or of moisture bridging the switch contacts; a grounded line could otherwise pass for a button held forever.
s: Fuel mode cannot be changed
Vehicle remains in one fuel mode
c: Switch signal wire chafed to ground behind the dash
Moisture or spilt liquid bridging the switch contacts

P25A7.d: P25A7 reports a fuel mode select switch signal above the accepted window. With a pull-up input this mostly means the switch never closes its path – an open signal or return wire, a connector half off, a broken switch – or that the line has contact with a supply voltage, for example where an alternative-fuel conversion tapped into nearby wiring.
s: Switch has no effect
Fuel indicator on the switch may stay dark
c: Open signal or return wire, connector not seated
Signal wire touching a supply voltage, e.g. after aftermarket wiring

P25A8.d: P25A8 records a fuel mode select switch signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying in a stable state. The module sees transitions it cannot attribute to a real press, often while driving over rough roads, which points to a loose terminal, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness rubbing behind the trim.
s: Occasional unexpected fuel mode changes
Switch light flickers
Code returns sporadically after clearing
c: Loose terminal or poor contact at the switch connector
Cracked solder joint inside the switch
Harness rubbing behind the trim and shorting briefly

P25A9.d: P25A9 covers the electrical circuit of the piston cooling oil control valve, the solenoid that switches the oil jets spraying the underside of the pistons. Under load the jets protect the pistons; when the engine is cold or lightly loaded they can be shut off to warm up faster and save oil pump work.
s: Check engine lamp on after two drives
Possible power reduction to protect the pistons
c: Valve connector unplugged, corroded or wire broken
Harness damaged by heat near the engine block
Output driver in the engine control module faulty

P25AA.d: P25AA flags a voltage at the piston cooling oil control valve output that sits too low for the commanded state, typically a short to ground between the module and the valve. This valve decides whether the oil jets under the pistons spray.
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Possible power limitation to protect the pistons
c: Valve control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the piston cooling valve
Water or oil in the valve connector bridging the pins
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P25AB.d: P25AB is the counterpart on the supply side: the control line of the piston cooling oil valve is pulled toward battery voltage. In GM's 18OBDG04 diesel table the check runs while the low-side driver is switched on; if the output then looks tied to power through 0.5 ohm or less, the module counts a short to power, again needing 40 failed samples out of 50 at 100 ms intervals with at least 11 V and logging a Type B fau
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Piston cooling jets no longer switched
Possible reduced engine power
c: Control wire pinched against a live supply wire
Valve side of the circuit shorted to its own supply
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P25AC.d: P25AC is a functional fault rather than a wiring one: the valve is told to let oil reach the piston jets, but the feedback shows no flow. GM's 18OBDG04 diesel table reads a pressure switch in the jet circuit and fails the test when that switch stays without pressure while the engine turns, main oil pressure is at least 206 kPa and the command has been held for 8 s or more; 40 of 50 samples must fail, Type B.
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Engine power reduced under high load
Risk of piston damage if driven hard for long periods
c: Valve jammed by swarf or dirt in the oil
Piston cooling pressure switch faulty or unplugged
Low oil level or weak oil pressure feeding the jet circuit
Restricted oil passage to the jets

P25AD.d: P25AD describes the reverse mechanical failure: the piston cooling valve ought to be shut, yet oil keeps reaching the jets. GM's diesel table 18OBDG04 detects it when the pressure switch in the jet circuit reports pressure although the valve has been commanded to its off state for at least 8 s, with the engine turning and main oil pressure of at least 206 kPa; 40 bad samples out of 50 make it a Type B fault.
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Longer warm-up in cold weather
Slightly lower oil pressure reading at idle
c: Broken return spring in the valve
Piston cooling pressure switch stuck in the pressure position

P25AE.d: P25AE means the oil pressure reaching the piston cooling jets is below what the engine controller requires, even though the valve circuit itself shows no electrical fault. Volvo and Mack heavy trucks store it as P25AE00.
s: Inactive code after heavy pulling
Low oil pressure warning at the same time
Engine derate possible
c: Oil temperature sensor reading wrong (Volvo/Mack bulletin)
Low oil level or oil starvation under hard load
Worn oil pump or leaking pressure relief valve
Clogged oil filter or piston cooling jets

P25AF.d: P25AF is a messenger code. A separate coolant temperature control module, used on some vehicles with electrically managed cooling for engine, battery or power electronics, has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to turn on the check engine lamp.
s: Check engine lamp on
Possible temperature warnings or reduced heating
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the coolant temperature control module
Faulty coolant valve, pump or sensor handled by that module
Thermal module software needing an update

P25B0.d: P25B0 means the main fuel level sender keeps reporting the same level although the engine has clearly been burning fuel. Ford runs this as a continuous check: the module totals the fuel injected, converts it into a share of tank capacity and compares that with how far the sender reading has moved.
s: Fuel gauge stays at the same mark over a long distance
Engine runs out of fuel while the gauge still shows fuel
Check engine lamp on
c: Float arm caught on the tank wall, baffle or pump module
Worn spot on the sender resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Float soaked with fuel and sunk to the bottom
Fuel consumption calculation in the PCM not matching the tank

P25B1.d: P25B1 points at the second fuel level sender, the one found in the passive half of a saddle tank or in an additional tank. Its reading no longer changes in step with the fuel actually burned.
s: Gauge reading too high or barely falling as the tank empties
Engine stalls from fuel starvation with an apparently quarter-full tank
Check engine lamp on
c: Float of sender B jammed or resistor track worn
Jet pump or its line no longer drawing fuel from the passive tank half
Blocked or kinked transfer line between the tank chambers

P25B2.d: P25B2 is the shared variant for tanks with two senders: the module has found that the level information is frozen but does not commit to which of the two senders is responsible. Ford lists it next to P25B0 and P25B1 under the same consumption-versus-reading check (100 to 120 miles, 25 to 60 % allowed mismatch) and, unlike the other two, keeps P25B2 as its own base code in the 2024 summary with failure type 00.
s: Gauge stuck or moving far less than fuel used
Range display unreliable
Check engine lamp on
c: One of the two senders mechanically stuck
Fuel no longer moved between tank halves by the jet pump
Corroded connector on the tank unit freezing one signal

P25B3.d: P25B3 says the wastegate of turbocharger A stays further open than the module commands, so exhaust bypasses the turbine and boost falls short. On Ford EcoBoost engines with an electric wastegate actuator and position sensor, the PCM compares commanded and measured position; a gap above 20 mm held for 2.5 s sets the code, provided no circuit fault (P0243, P2ABD) is present.
s: Clearly reduced power and slow boost build-up
Check engine lamp on, often with an underboost code
Wrench or reduced power warning on some models
c: Missing retaining clip disconnecting actuator rod from the wastegate lever
Electric wastegate actuator failed or rod bent
Wastegate flap or bushing seized in the open position by heat or carbon
Diagnostic calibration needing an update (Toyota GR Corolla)

P25B4.d: P25B4 is the reverse of P25B3: the module asked wastegate A to open, yet the valve stays shut or opens far too little. Ford uses the same position comparison for both directions (error over 20 mm for 2.5 s); in 2024 it appears as P0243 with failure type 73.
s: Power reduced because the module limits boost
Possible overboost code alongside
Check engine lamp on
c: Wastegate flap or spindle seized shut by carbon or corrosion
Actuator or linkage unable to move the valve
False detection by engine software (Porsche Cayenne, Audi RS 5)
Internal turbocharger fault requiring replacement (Ford SSM 50670)

P25B5.d: P25B5 concerns wastegate B, which on twin-turbo V engines belongs to the second turbocharger, normally on the other cylinder bank. The valve remains open beyond what the PCM commands, so this turbo delivers too little boost while the A side may work normally.
s: Reduced power, especially when accelerating under load
Check engine lamp and/or wrench indicator on
c: Wastegate B linkage loose or disconnected
Actuator B failed or its position sensor reading wrong
Flap of wastegate B seized open

P25B6.d: With P25B6 the second wastegate refuses to open when commanded, so turbo B cannot be regulated down and may push boost beyond the target; the module then usually caps torque. Ford detects it with the B-side position comparison (over 20 mm for 2.5 s, no P0247 or P2ABE present) and in 2024 files it as P0247 with type 73.
s: Power limited, sometimes after a short boost spike
Check engine lamp on, possibly with P0299 or an overboost code
c: Loose nut on the turbo actuator arm (Ford Bronco TSB 24-2112)
Wastegate B flap or spindle seized shut
Actuator B unable to drive the valve open

P25B7.d: P25B7 covers the hard-wired input from an auxiliary ignition switch that commands the On and Start positions from a second location, for example a rear panel behind the cab, a work platform or a remote station on a chassis-cab truck. The module flags a state on this line it cannot interpret, such as an open circuit, without saying whether the level is too low or too high.
s: Engine cannot be started or switched on from the auxiliary position
Normal key or push-button start still works
Stored code, often without other complaints
c: Open wire or loose connector in the harness to the body or remote panel
Worn or corroded contacts in the auxiliary switch
Input stage of the reading module damaged

P25B8.d: P25B8 means the auxiliary On/Start input sits at a low level when the module expects it to be active, or never rises when the remote switch is operated. Typical reasons are a switch contact that no longer closes, a blown fuse feeding the remote panel, a broken wire in the long harness run to the body or a short to ground at a frame connector.
s: Remote start or on request is ignored
Engine may shut down when the auxiliary position is used to keep it running
Remote panel indicator stays dark
c: Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the auxiliary switch
Signal wire shorted to ground on the frame or body
Auxiliary switch contact no longer closes
Corroded exterior connector with high resistance

P25B9.d: With P25B9 the module sees the auxiliary On/Start line at a high level when it ought to be inactive, for example after key-off or with no request from the remote panel. A switch stuck in the start position, a wire rubbing against a battery feed, backfeed through an upfitter relay or moisture bridging terminals in an exterior switch box can all hold the line up.
s: Battery drains overnight because modules stay awake
Auxiliary start function disabled or behaving erratically
Starter may engage or click unexpectedly
c: Signal wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Auxiliary switch stuck in the On/Start position
Backfeed through an upfitter relay or accessory
Moisture in an exterior switch box or connector

P25BA.d: P25BA concerns the dash or panel switch with which the driver starts, or on some trucks blocks, a diesel particulate filter regeneration. The engine controller reads the switch as a discrete input and sets this code when the circuit is open or otherwise unusable, so a press no longer reaches it.
s: Parked regeneration cannot be started when the cluster asks for it
Filter or regeneration warning lamp stays on longer than usual
Check engine lamp
c: Switch connector loose or unplugged behind the dash
Broken signal or reference wire to the switch
Internal open circuit in the regeneration switch

P25BB.d: P25BB reports that the regeneration switch input reads a low level the switch itself cannot produce. Depending on the wiring, this points to a short to ground in the harness, a contact that is permanently closed to ground or a damaged switch module.
s: Regeneration switch has no effect
Parked regeneration may be unavailable when soot load is high
Check engine lamp
c: Switch signal wire shorted to ground
Switch panel damaged by liquid or impact

P25BC.d: P25BC is the high-voltage counterpart: the regeneration switch line carries a level near supply voltage that no switch position can produce. A wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed, water in a switch connector or a switch whose internal resistor network has failed are plausible causes.
s: Regeneration switch ignored by the engine controller
Unexpected regeneration messages in the cluster
Check engine lamp
c: Switch signal wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Internal fault in the switch or its resistor network

P25BD.d: P25BD protects against engine runaway, where the engine keeps speeding up although the controller injects no fuel, for instance because oil from a failed turbocharger seal or combustible vapour drawn into the intake is being burned. GM documents the monitor in its diesel ECM tables.
s: Engine revs up uncontrollably and then shuts off
Heavy smoke from the exhaust before shutdown
Check engine lamp on immediately
Possible severe engine damage after the event
c: Turbocharger seal failure feeding oil into the intake
Oil carry-over from crankcase ventilation, e.g. overfilled or diluted oil
Combustible vapour drawn in from the surroundings
Erroneous engine speed signal or controller fault

P25BE.d: P25BE concerns the output with which the engine controller tells an alternative fuel system, usually a CNG or LPG installation, to stop gas operation, for example after a fault, with an empty gas tank or while the engine warms up. The code reports an open circuit or a driver fault on this control line, so the command may no longer reach the gas controller or its shut-off valves.
s: Vehicle stays on gasoline or will not switch to gas
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a system fault
Check engine lamp
c: Open control wire between engine controller and gas system
Poor splice or connector in a retrofit gas installation
Open coil in a gas disable relay
Output driver in the engine controller defective

P25BF.d: P25BF flags a voltage on the alternative fuel disable output that is too high for the state the engine controller is commanding. On a low-side driver this usually means a short to battery or ignition voltage, for instance where a gas kit harness has been routed along a hot feed or tapped into the wrong wire.
s: Gas operation blocked, vehicle runs on gasoline only
Fuel mode indicator flashes
Check engine lamp
c: Control wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Retrofit gas kit tapped into the wrong circuit
Faulty input stage in the gas controller backfeeding voltage

P25C0.d: P25C0 is set when the alternative fuel disable output reads too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the engine controller and the gas system. With a high-side driver that pin would then be unable to deliver its voltage; with a low-side driver the line would look permanently switched.
s: Vehicle refuses to switch to gas
Fuel system fault message or flashing fuel indicator
Check engine lamp
c: Control wire shorted to ground, often where routed along the frame
Chafed insulation on a retrofit gas kit harness
Output stage in the engine controller damaged

P25C1.d: P25C1 relates to the incoming side of the alternative fuel disable function: a signal line on which the engine controller reads whether gas operation is blocked, either as feedback from the gas system or as a request from it, for example when a CNG or LPG controller detects low tank pressure or its own fault. The code says the signal is missing or unusable without naming a direction.
s: Gas mode unavailable or drops out while driving
Fuel mode indicator flashes
Check engine lamp
c: Open signal wire from the gas system
Gas controller without power or ground, so no signal is sent
Corroded underbody connector of the gas system

P25C2.d: P25C2 means the alternative fuel disable signal arriving at the engine controller sits above its valid range. Likely explanations are a short to a voltage feed, a missing ground at the gas controller that lets its output float up, or an open line combined with an internal pull-up in the reading module.
s: Vehicle stays on gasoline
Gas system fault indication
Check engine lamp
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage feed
Missing ground at the gas controller letting its output float high
Open signal wire pulled up inside the reading module

P25C3.d: P25C3 is logged when the alternative fuel disable signal reaching the engine controller is too low to be valid. A short to ground on the way from the gas system, a gas controller that has lost its supply, or a damaged output stage in that controller can each pull the line down.
s: No change-over to gas operation
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
Check engine lamp
c: Damaged output stage in the gas controller

P25C4.d: P25C4 covers the first temperature sensor of an electromechanical brake booster, in which an electric motor and gear set take the place of the vacuum diaphragm, as in Bosch's iBooster. The booster electronics use this value to protect motor and control unit from overheating during long or repeated braking.
s: Brake system warning in the cluster
Brake pedal may feel harder if assistance is reduced
Stored code, often together with chassis codes
c: Temperature sensor inside the booster unit defective
Fault in the booster control electronics

P25C5.d: P25C5 is the plausibility fault for brake booster temperature sensor A: the circuit is electrically intact, but the reported temperature does not fit, for example a value that jumps implausibly, stays frozen while the motor works hard, or disagrees with the second sensor. No manufacturer documents P25C5 publicly.
s: Brake warning message, sometimes only after long braking
Brake assistance reduced as a precaution
c: Sensor drifted out of its characteristic curve
Contact resistance at the booster connector skewing the signal
Measurement error in the booster electronics

P25C6.d: P25C6 means the signal of brake booster temperature sensor A is too low, which GM describes as the sensor line being shorted to ground. GM uses the code on the 2023 Corvette Z06 (table 23OBDG07, EBCM section) and keeps the same logic in its 2024 and 2025 tables 24OBDG07 and 25OBDG03A: the check runs continuously with the ignition on, needs the condition five times in a row within 0.6 s and is rated Type B, so the MIL
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Brake system warning message
Brake assistance may be limited
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the temperature sensor

P25C7.d: P25C7 flags a sensor A signal that is too high; GM interprets it as the temperature line shorted to supply. In the EBCM part of table 23OBDG07 for the 2023 Corvette Z06 the voltage must exceed 3.27 V five consecutive times within 0.6 s with the ignition on, and the fault is Type B with two trips to the MIL.
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Brake system warning message
Reduced brake assistance possible
c: Sensor signal shorted to the supply line
Open sensor circuit or missing sensor ground

P25C8.d: P25C8 is meant for a sensor A signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than any real temperature in the booster could change, the typical footprint of a loose pin, a cracked solder joint or a wire that breaks under vibration. Each event may be too short for the low or high check to confirm, which is why this separate code exists.
s: Brake warning that appears and disappears
Occasional change in pedal feel
c: Loose or spread terminal in the booster connector
Cracked solder joint inside the booster electronics

P25C9.d: P25C9 tells the engine module that a second brake system control module, labelled B, has found an emission-relevant malfunction and wants the check engine lamp switched on. GM uses the code in its hybrid OBD tables 16OBDG01, 18OBDG01 and 19OBDG01: the engine module listens to the lamp request message from module B continuously, starting three seconds after power-up, and logs P25C9 as Type A but without its own lamp r
s: Check engine lamp on
Brake or stability warnings at the same time
c: Fault stored in brake system control module B
Weak battery or low system voltage
Communication fault between module B and its partners

P25CA.d: Some cam phasers carry a locking pin that holds the rotor in a fixed base or middle position for starting and while oil pressure is still building. Where that pin is released and engaged by its own solenoid, the controller supervises this extra circuit.
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough start or unsteady idle
Intake cam timing held at a default position, less power
c: Open winding in the intake phaser lock solenoid
Connector off or terminal pushed back after engine work
Broken wire between module and lock solenoid

P25CB.d: P25CB points to a control line for the intake phaser lock on bank 1 that reads lower than it should, most often a short to ground on the wire or inside the lock solenoid. Depending on how the driver is wired, the solenoid may then stay energised or never receive current, so the lock pin is either released all the time or cannot be pulled back.
s: Check engine lamp on
Brief rattle from the timing drive at start
Reduced power with fixed intake timing
c: Lock control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the lock solenoid
Weak battery or voltage dip during cranking

P25CC.d: With P25CC the controller sees the intake phaser lock control line on bank 1 sitting higher than expected, typically because it touches a live wire or the solenoid's ground path is shorted to supply. A protected output stage usually shuts down when it detects this, which leaves the lock solenoid without control: the pin falls back to whatever its spring dictates, and the intake phaser is then often parked at its lock
s: Check engine lamp on
Sluggish response with intake timing fixed
c: Lock control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Harness insulation melted near the exhaust or turbo
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P25CD.d: P25CD is the bank 2 version of the open-circuit lock fault and therefore only appears on V or boxer engines whose second cylinder bank has its own intake phaser with a separately switched lock pin. The controller finds the lock solenoid circuit on that bank interrupted or electrically implausible, so it can no longer release or set the pin deliberately.
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle
Less power, bank 2 intake timing fixed
c: Open circuit inside the bank 2 lock solenoid
Bank 2 lock solenoid connector unplugged or corroded
Wire break in the harness across the engine

P25CE.d: P25CE stands for a low signal on the lock control line of the bank 2 intake phaser: the wire or the solenoid winding has found a path to ground, or the module's output is stuck pulling low. Because the second bank's harness often runs along the back of the engine or under the intake manifold, chafing at brackets and heat damage are frequent findings.
s: Check engine lamp on
Clatter at cold start
c: Bank 2 harness chafed through at a bracket
Shorted winding in the bank 2 lock solenoid
Low system voltage setting lock codes on both banks

P25CF.d: P25CF is logged when the bank 2 intake phaser lock control line stays above its permitted voltage band. Common reasons are contact with a powered wire, moisture bridging connector pins to a supply terminal, or a failed output transistor in the controller.
s: Check engine lamp on
Lumpy idle from uneven bank timing
c: Bank 2 lock control wire touching a powered circuit
Moisture in the connector bridging to a supply pin
Failed output transistor in the engine control module

P25D0.d: P25D0 moves the open-circuit lock fault to the exhaust side: the solenoid that releases the locking pin of the bank 1 exhaust cam phaser can no longer be driven because its circuit is interrupted or reads implausibly. The lock keeps the exhaust cam at a defined position while the engine starts, before the phaser has enough oil pressure to hold itself.
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Rough idle possible
c: Open winding in the exhaust phaser lock solenoid
Broken wire to the exhaust lock solenoid

P25D1.d: P25D1 indicates that the control signal for the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock is too low, normally a grounded wire or a solenoid winding that leaks to ground. The exhaust side is the hotter one, so insulation that has hardened and cracked near the manifold or turbocharger is a typical finding.
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust timing fixed, slightly less power
c: Heat-cracked insulation grounding the lock wire
Engine oil wicked into the connector

P25D2.d: P25D2 is set when the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock control line carries more voltage than the controller allows in the current switching state, for example because it is shorted to an ignition-fed wire or the solenoid's return is tied to supply. Most output stages detect overcurrent here and switch off, so the lock solenoid loses its command and the pin goes to the position its spring defines.
s: Check engine lamp on
Weaker mid-range pull
c: Lock control wire shorted to an ignition-fed circuit
Solenoid return path shorted to supply
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P25D3.d: P25D3 concerns engines with two cylinder banks and a lockable exhaust phaser on each: the lock solenoid circuit of the bank 2 exhaust phaser is open or electrically implausible, so the module loses control over its pin. On many V engines the bank 2 exhaust solenoid sits at the rear or close to the firewall, where connectors are easily left loose after timing work.
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven running between the banks
c: Bank 2 exhaust lock connector left loose after timing work
Open winding in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid
Open in a supply shared with other phaser solenoids

P25D4.d: P25D4 reports a lock control line for the bank 2 exhaust phaser that is pulled down below its expected level. Grounding through damaged insulation, a solenoid with shorted turns or oil that has crept into the connector are the usual explanations.
s: Check engine lamp on
Bank 2 exhaust timing fixed
c: Heat sleeve slipped, wire grounded at the manifold
Shorted turns in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid

P25D5.d: P25D5 closes this series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser's lock control signal sits above its allowed voltage, pointing to a short to battery or ignition voltage, a return path tied to supply, or a defective output in the module. The protected driver then stops switching, and the lock solenoid stays without command until the next key cycle or until the fault vanishes.
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption
c: Bank 2 exhaust lock wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness fault affecting several actuator lines
Defective output in the engine control module

P25D6.d: An exhaust heat exchanger moves exhaust heat into the coolant after a cold start; a flap (bypass valve A) decides whether gas flows through it or around it, and a position sensor reports where the flap is. P25D6 targets the end-stop values of that sensor: at the fully open and fully closed stops the reading must sit inside a learned or calibrated window.
s: Check engine lamp on without noticeable driving change
Slower engine warm-up or weaker cabin heat in winter
c: Carbon build-up or a bent flap stopping short of its end stop
Worn valve actuator or linkage play
Position sensor shifted on its mount or drifting
End stops not relearned after parts replacement

P25D7.d: Fuel level sensor C is a third level input, needed only where the fuel is spread over more chambers or tanks than two senders can cover, for instance on trucks with an extra tank. P25D7 is its general circuit code: the module sees an electrical fault on this input but does not classify it as low, high or intermittent.
s: Gauge or range wrong or replaced by a default value
Check engine lamp on
c: Damaged wiring between tank C sender and module, often under the vehicle
Corroded or loose connector at the sender

P25D8.d: P25D8 says that the third fuel level input delivers an electrically valid signal whose behaviour is not believable: it jumps, drifts or disagrees with the fuel actually used or transferred. A sender frozen at one value has its own code, P25DC, so P25D8 covers the remaining plausibility faults.
s: Fuel gauge jumps or shows unrealistic values
Range estimate inconsistent
Check engine lamp on after repeated detection
c: Worn or dirty resistor track in sender C giving jumps
Transfer pump or line fault so the level in tank C does not change as expected
Damaged or loose float on sender C

P25D9.d: P25D9 reports that the signal of the third fuel level sender has dropped below its lowest valid value. With the usual resistor-type sender this points to very low resistance, typically a signal wire shorted to ground or a sender shorted internally.
s: Gauge pinned at full or empty
Check engine lamp on
c: Signal wire of sender C chafed and shorted to ground
Water in the tank connector bridging signal and ground

P25DA.d: P25DA is set when the third sender's signal climbs above the top of its valid range. On a resistor sender fed through a pull-up, that almost always means an open path: a broken wire, a disconnected plug, a burnt-out spot on the resistor track or a missing ground return.
s: Gauge stuck at one end of the scale
Check engine lamp on
c: Broken signal or ground wire to sender C
Tank connector loose or unplugged after work on the tank
Interrupted resistor track inside sender C
Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply

P25DB.d: P25DB describes short, repeated dropouts in the third fuel level input: the signal leaves its valid range for moments and returns, rather than staying low or high. Typical culprits are a loose pin, a wire that breaks contact only when the vehicle flexes or the tank moves, and a sender whose wiper briefly lifts off the resistor track over rough roads.
s: Fuel gauge flickers or drops briefly to empty
Check engine lamp may come and go
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sender C connector
Wire breaking contact when the frame or tank moves
Sender wiper lifting off a worn resistor track

P25DC.d: P25DC is set when a third fuel level sender, sender C, keeps returning the same reading although the engine has consumed a meaningful amount of fuel. Such a third input exists only on vehicles with extra or divided tanks, for example saddle tanks or auxiliary tanks on trucks.
s: Fuel gauge or range display frozen over a long distance
Risk of running out of fuel despite a displayed reserve
Check engine lamp on
c: Float arm of sender C caught on a baffle, pump bracket or tank wall
Worn spot on the sender C resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Fuel transfer to or from tank C not working, so its level really does not change

P25DD.d: Many modern cam phasers hold their rotor with a spring-loaded pin at a defined angle, often in mid travel, so the engine starts with stable valve timing before oil pressure builds. P25DD means the intake phaser on bank 1 is still latched at that angle although the controller has asked it to unlock and move, so variable timing is lost on that camshaft.
s: Check engine lamp on
Less pulling power, especially in the mid-speed range
Higher fuel consumption
c: Low oil level or pressure, or oil of the wrong viscosity, unable to push the pin out
Oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser sticking or its screen clogged
Lock pin seized in its bore by sludge or wear inside the phaser

P25DE.d: P25DE is the reverse of P25DD: the intake cam phaser on bank 1 should return to its lock angle and let the pin engage, typically as the engine is about to stop or idles before an automatic stop, but the controller never sees the expected locked position. If the pin is not in place at the next start, the rotor can rattle against its stops and timing wanders until oil pressure takes over.
s: Check engine lamp on
Short rattle or knock from the timing drive right after starting
Rough start or unsteady idle in the first seconds
c: Debris or wear in the phaser keeping the pin from dropping into its slot
Oil control valve sticking so the lock range of the spool is never reached
Aged or contaminated oil slowing the phaser at hot idle

P25DF.d: P25DF belongs to the same block as the lock codes P25DD and P25DE, but it does not describe the latch itself. It flags that the intake phaser on bank 1 is not following its commanded angle as well as the calibration expects, judged as a check of control quality rather than as a plain deviation toward early or late timing (P0011, P0012) or a slow response (P000A).
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle or slight hesitation when accelerating
Somewhat higher fuel consumption
c: Worn or partly clogged oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser
Oil overdue, diluted or of the wrong grade
Internal leakage in the phaser letting the angle drift

P25E0.d: On engines with two cylinder banks, P25E0 is the bank 2 counterpart of P25DD: the intake camshaft actuator stays latched at its locking angle when the module wants it free to advance or retard. Because only one side is affected, the cam angles of the two banks no longer match, and the module may hold both sides in a fallback position.
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power and rough idle
Higher fuel consumption
c: Insufficient oil pressure at the bank 2 head, low level or clogged feed screen
Bank 2 intake oil control valve sticking
Lock pin mechanically jammed in the phaser

P25E1.d: P25E1 is set when the intake phaser on bank 2 fails to re-engage its lock. The controller commands the phaser toward the locking angle, usually when shutting down or before an idle stop, and then checks whether the measured cam angle settles there; on bank 2 it does not.
s: Check engine lamp on
Brief rattle from the timing drive on start-up
Unsteady running right after a cold or warm start
c: Low oil pressure at hot idle from worn pump, bearings or thin oil
Varnish or debris in the bank 2 intake phaser
Control valve unable to move the spool into its lock range

P25E2.d: P25E2 points to poor position control of the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator: the measured angle tracks its target less accurately or with more oscillation than the calibration allows, while no clear lock fault is present. It is the bank 2 sibling of P25DF.
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly unsteady idle
Lower fuel economy
c: Bank 2 intake solenoid valve worn or sluggish
Internal leakage across the phaser vanes

P25E3.d: P25E3 concerns the exhaust side: the bank 1 exhaust phaser, camshaft B, remains held by its lock pin when the controller wants to move it. Exhaust timing then stays at its parking angle, which limits how the module can use valve overlap for internal exhaust gas recirculation and scavenging.
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough idle
Slight loss of power, possibly failed emissions test
c: Low or contaminated oil at the exhaust phaser
Bank 1 exhaust oil control valve sticking
Damaged rotor or lock pin inside the exhaust phaser

P25E4.d: P25E4 means the bank 1 exhaust phaser does not reach and engage its locking position when the controller asks for it, for example before shutdown or an automatic engine stop. Stellantis lists P25E4 in several PCM reflash bulletins for Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer models with the 3.0-litre Hurricane high-output twin-turbo inline six and stop-start, among them 18-022-25 Rev.
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop, restarts after an ignition cycle
Rough start
c: Engine control software needing an update (documented for Stellantis Hurricane engines)
Low oil pressure at hot idle so the phaser cannot swing into the lock
Debris in the exhaust phaser or a sticking control valve

P25E5.d: P25E5 reports that the exhaust camshaft actuator on bank 1 is controlled less precisely than intended: its angle lags, overshoots or oscillates around the target beyond calibrated limits, without a latch fault. It is the exhaust-side counterpart of P25DF and overlaps in meaning with P0014 and the slow-response code P000B; no manufacturer documents how P25E5 is told apart from them.
s: Check engine lamp on
Unsteady idle
Slightly reduced power or economy
c: Worn or dirty control valve for the bank 1 exhaust phaser
Degraded engine oil or a blocked oil filter
Noisy exhaust camshaft position signal making the angle look unstable

P25E6.d: P25E6 tells that on bank 2 the exhaust cam phaser has not left its locked angle despite a command to adjust. The module then has one exhaust camshaft that can no longer be phased, which shifts valve overlap on that bank and can upset idle quality and the emissions balance between the two banks.
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power, uneven idle
Rattle from the timing drive
c: Restricted oil feed or clogged screen to the bank 2 cylinder head
Bank 2 exhaust oil control valve stuck
Lock pin seized in the bank 2 exhaust phaser

P25E7.d: With P25E7 the module reports that the bank 2 exhaust phaser could not be brought into its locking position: when the lock is requested, the cam angle does not settle at the parking value or the pin does not hold it there. A start without the pin engaged tends to be rough, and on stop-start engines a smooth restart becomes less certain.
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough or rattling start
Hesitant restart after an automatic engine stop
c: Aged or sludged oil slowing the bank 2 exhaust phaser
Spool of the bank 2 exhaust control valve hanging
Worn lock pin or pin bore so the pin no longer holds
Calibration issue fixed by a control unit update

P25E8.d: P25E8 is the last code of the locked-position block and covers the control quality of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator: the module sees the angle wander from, overshoot or trail its setpoint more than allowed, while lock-related faults are absent. Older codes such as P0024 and P000D describe similar exhaust deviations on bank 2; which one a given calibration uses is not documented publicly by any manufacturer, so
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle
Higher fuel use
c: Wear in the bank 2 exhaust control valve
Wrong oil viscosity or a clogged oil filter
Worn rotor seals inside the exhaust phaser

P25E9.d: Some engines drive their mechanical supercharger through an electromagnetic clutch, so the blower only turns when extra low-speed torque is wanted. Eaton's TVS blower on the T6 Drive-E four-cylinder from Volvo is built this way, where the turbocharger takes over at higher revs.
s: Check engine lamp on
Weak acceleration from low engine speed
Normal pull once the turbocharger takes over
c: Worn friction faces or too large an air gap, so the clutch slips or will not pull in
Clutch coil with an internal fault producing too little magnetic force
Low supply voltage or high resistance at the clutch connector
Accessory drive belt slipping or damaged at the supercharger pulley

P25EA.d: Here the clutch between pulley and supercharger rotors stays engaged although the engine computer wants the blower uncoupled, for example at idle or steady cruising. The blower then keeps turning, costs drive power and fuel, and its air has to be routed past it.
s: Check engine lamp on
Higher fuel consumption at part load
Supercharger whine also at idle or cruising
c: Engine control software misjudging the clutch state (Audi Q7 3.0 TFSI, bulletin 2048402)
Clutch plates stuck together by wear debris, corrosion or overheating
Clutch coil kept energised by a wiring fault or a stuck driver stage

P25EB.d: P25EB covers the electrical drive of the supercharger clutch when it is neither cleanly shorted nor open, yet the values do not fit the command – for example a coil current that is too small or too large for the applied duty cycle, or a signal that drops out briefly. According to Eaton, the clutch needs only a 12 V signal but is engaged with a modulated signal so that it bites smoothly, which gives the controller som
s: Check engine lamp on
Jerky or missing supercharger engagement at low revs
c: Clutch coil whose resistance has changed through heat or partial winding short
Corroded or loose connector at the clutch or engine module
Wire chafed near the hot supercharger housing causing intermittent contact

P25EC.d: The engine module measures a voltage on the supercharger clutch control line that is lower than expected for the commanded state. Most often the line has a short to ground.
s: Check engine lamp on
Supercharger permanently engaged or permanently off, depending on circuit design
Reduced power at low engine speed
c: Control wire shorted to ground, often chafed on brackets or the engine block
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P25ED.d: With P25ED the voltage on the clutch control line sits above the expected level. Common reasons are a wire shorted to battery voltage, or – on a ground-switched coil – an open coil or broken lead, because the line is then pulled up to supply voltage.
s: Check engine lamp on
Sluggish pull-away, supercharger does not cut in
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open clutch coil or broken wire on a ground-switched circuit
Output stage in the engine control module damaged

P25EE.d: P25EE covers the second control circuit of an electric brake vacuum pump, the part of the wiring that should carry voltage while the pump is switched on. Ford's 2019 OBD summary for its hybrid and plug-in models assigns P25EE to the brake system module, mapped from that module's own code C1036: with the pump relay commanded closed, a monitoring line voltage below 250 mV for one second means the pump is not getting it
s: Hard brake pedal, especially with the engine off or in electric drive
Brake or traction warning lamp in addition to the check engine lamp
Vacuum pump never heard running
c: Broken wire or loose connector between relay and pump

P25EF.d: P25EF says that the B circuit driving the electric vacuum pump is electrically present but its behaviour does not match the command: the feedback on the switched side looks implausible, or the pump runs without the expected effect on brake vacuum. No manufacturer documents P25EF publicly.
s: Brake pedal firmer than normal
Vacuum pump running longer or more often
Warning lamp on
c: Worn vacuum pump that runs but builds too little vacuum
Leaking vacuum hose or faulty check valve
Corroded terminals causing an unstable feedback voltage

P25F0.d: P25F0 is stored when the pump's B control circuit reads lower than expected, usually because the switched supply or feedback line is shorted to ground or loaded down by a pump motor with an internal short. A short to ground on the supply side often blows the pump fuse, so the pump then stops altogether.
s: Hard brake pedal
Repeatedly blown vacuum pump fuse
Warning lamp on
c: Chafed supply or feedback wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the vacuum pump motor
Water ingress in the pump connector

P25F1.d: P25F1 marks a high reading on the vacuum pump's second (B) control circuit: the module sees voltage on the switched side when it should be low, for example because the line is shorted to battery voltage, the relay contacts have welded together or the pump has lost its ground. In the welded-relay case the pump keeps running after it has been switched off, which wears it out and drains the battery.
s: Vacuum pump running constantly, even with the vehicle switched off
Discharged 12 V battery
Warning lamp on
c: Feedback or supply line shorted to battery voltage
Lost ground connection at the pump

P25F2.d: A third boost pressure sensor, C, only makes sense on engines with several charging stages or chargers – for example a supercharger feeding a turbocharger, or a two-stage turbo system – where pressure is measured between the stages as well as ahead of the throttle. Which location carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer.
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power, boost limited to base level
c: Loose, corroded or oily connector at boost sensor C
Signal, 5 V reference or ground wire damaged

P25F3.d: P25F3 means boost sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but does not agree with what the other pressure readings and the engine model suggest. Saab's 2.0 litre turbo engine, developed with GM, shows how this is checked for sensor A: with the engine stopped the reading must lie between 50 and 115 kPa, roughly matching barometric pressure, and while running it is compared with a model built from baromet
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power under load
Hissing noise if a charge air leak is present
c: Charge air leak near the measuring point of sensor C (hose, clamp, seal)
Sensor port fouled by oil from crankcase ventilation or a drifting sensor
Faulty barometric or manifold pressure sensor skewing the comparison

P25F4.d: Boost pressure sensors of this kind output a voltage that rises with pressure, so P25F4 – a signal below the lowest valid value – points to the wiring or the sensor rather than to the charge air. Usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing 5 V supply, or an open signal line on an input pulled down by the control unit.
s: Check engine lamp on
Noticeable loss of power
Scan tool shows a pressure far below ambient for sensor C
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another faulty sensor on the same supply

P25F5.d: P25F5 reports a signal from boost sensor C above the highest plausible value. Since the voltage climbs with pressure, a reading at the top end usually means an electrical fault: the signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or an open signal wire where the input is pulled up.
s: Check engine lamp on, depending on the manufacturer
Reduced power, boost cut back
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P25F6.d: P25F6 is the overall monitor for a second secondary air injection system, lettered B, on engines with two separately controlled air delivery paths; system A reports through P0410 and P0411. During warm-up after a cold start a pump pushes fresh air into the exhaust, so leftover HC and CO burn off and the catalyst lights off sooner.
s: MIL on, usually after a cold start
Secondary air readiness monitor not complete, emissions test failed
Unusual whining or no pump noise during the first minute after a cold start
c: Secondary air pump of system B worn, seized or water-damaged
Switching or check valve of system B stuck, often after debris from the pump
Cracked, loose or disconnected air hose or vacuum line
Faulty pump relay, fuse or wiring of system B

P25F7.d: With P25F7 the engine controller finds that the air delivered by secondary air system B does not match its expectation while the system is switched on after a cold start. Depending on the design, it judges the flow from how the oxygen sensors on that side react, from a pressure sensor in the air line or from pump behaviour.
s: MIL on after one or two cold starts
Emissions test failed or readiness incomplete
Driveability normally unchanged
c: Air pump of system B delivers too little air
Switching or check valve fouled or stuck partly closed
Air passages to the exhaust restricted by carbon deposits
Leaking air hose so that part of the flow escapes

P25F8.d: Bypass valves in the intake let charge air flow around a compressor: on turbo engines they are the recirculation valves that open on a sudden throttle lift so the compressor does not surge, and on engines with a supercharger they can route air past the blower while it is idling or uncoupled. A third such valve, C, only appears on systems with several compressors; which valve gets the letter is manufacturer-specific.
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering noise when lifting off the throttle
Less boost or slower response
c: Broken wire or loose connector at bypass valve C
Open coil in the valve or its solenoid

P25F9.d: P25F9 tells that the control line of bypass valve C reads too low a voltage, normally because it touches ground somewhere or the coil is shorted. If the engine module switches the valve on the ground side, a grounded wire leaves the valve energised all the time; on an electric recirculation valve, which according to Pierburg works without a vacuum line, that means charge air keeps escaping back to the compressor inle
s: Check engine lamp on
Too little boost if the valve stays open
Surging or fluttering on lift-off if it stays shut
c: Output stage in the engine control module faulty

P25FA.d: With P25FA the control line of bypass valve C carries more voltage than the engine module expects for the commanded state. A wire shorted to battery voltage is the classic reason; on a ground-switched valve an open coil or broken lead also lets the line float up to supply level.
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open valve coil on a ground-switched circuit
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P25FB.d: P25FB is set when the control circuit of bypass valve C is not open or shorted, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command – for instance a current that rises too slowly or settles at the wrong level, or a signal that drops out now and then. That points to a coil whose resistance has changed with heat, contact resistance in the connector, or a valve whose armature moves sluggishly and so alters the curre
s: Check engine lamp on
Occasional fluttering on lift-off
Uneven boost build-up
c: Valve coil resistance changed by heat ageing
Contact resistance or moisture in the valve connector
Sluggish valve armature due to deposits

P25FC.d: P25FC concerns the valve itself, not its wiring: bypass valve C is electrically in order but does not move as commanded, sticking open, shut or somewhere in between. A valve stuck open lets charge air leak back to the compressor inlet, so boost falls short; one stuck shut cannot relieve pressure when the throttle closes, and the compressor surges audibly.
s: Check engine lamp on
Loud fluttering when lifting off the throttle
Lack of boost and power
c: Oil and soot deposits from crankcase ventilation jamming the valve
Torn diaphragm or broken spring inside the valve
Cracked valve housing or leaking seal

P25FD.d: This code says bypass valve C has become too hot. Recirculation valves are placed in the charge air path close to the compressor and thus near the hot turbine side, and an electric valve's coil adds its own heat when energised for long periods.
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering on lift-off or reduced boost after hard driving
c: Heat soak from the turbocharger, e.g. after hard driving or with missing heat shields
Valve coil drawing too much current due to an internal fault
Sluggish valve held energised longer than intended

P25FE.d: P25FE is the umbrella code for the supercharger disconnect clutch: it says the clutch function has failed without naming whether it is stuck, slipping or electrically faulty. Those cases have their own codes – P25E9 and P25EA for the mechanical states, P25EB to P25ED for the control circuit – so a control unit that sets P25FE either does not distinguish them or uses it as a summary.
s: Check engine lamp on
Weak response at low engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
c: Worn or seized clutch on the supercharger pulley
Fault in the coil, wiring or connector of the clutch
Engine control software that misjudges the clutch state

P25FF.d: P25FF reports that the module which steadies the 12 V supply for sensitive electronics does not work as intended. Such stabilizers mainly appear on cars with automatic engine stop/start: every restart drags the battery voltage down hard, according to a semiconductor maker briefly below 4 V, which would otherwise reset radios, displays and similar loads.
s: Automatic stop/start no longer active
Radio or display resets when the engine restarts
Warning light depending on the maker
c: Internal fault in the voltage stabilizer or DC/DC converter module
Aged or wrong-type 12 V battery so the module cannot hold the voltage
Current backfeed or poor supply/ground connection at the module
